about: Every Claude Code behavior csift depends on, one claim per entry. Each check names the instrument that ran, what it observed and the counting rule; the README badge version is admitted only when every claim carries a check at that version. Never bulk-edit the checks.

claims.behavior: A backgrounded shell launch is an ordinary `type:"assistant"` record carrying a `Bash` (on Windows `PowerShell`) `tool_use` whose input is `{command, description?, timeout?, run_in_background:true, dangerouslyDisableSandbox?}`. Across 2942 corpus launches `description` was present on 99.4% and `timeout` on 25.0%. The flag is NOT exclusive to the two shell tools (the `Agent` tool takes it too, 257 launches) and it is NOT the only way into the background: a FOREGROUND shell command that exceeds its timeout is auto-moved to the background, minting a `backgroundTaskId` with no `run_in_background` on the launching tool_use (80 corpus cases, CC 2.1.210 through 2.1.258).
claims.depends: csift's launch ingester keys on exactly that shape (tool name `Bash` or `PowerShell` plus `input.run_in_background == true`); a renamed input flag would make every background task invisible and collapse the `idle-background-open` verdict.

claims.behavior: The paired `tool_result` for a backgrounded shell opens `Command running in background with ID: <id>. Output is being written to: <abs path>.` and then appends, conditionally, ONE of two notify sentences (`You will be notified when it completes.` on 97.2% of corpus results, or `If it exits while you are still working you will be notified, but it is terminated when you give your final response...` on 1.0%) or neither (1.8%), then usually `To check interim output, use Read on that file path.`, then optionally a `Session cwd remains <path>; directory changes made by the backgrounded command do not apply to subsequent commands.` line (34.0%). The structured `toolUseResult` is `{stdout, stderr, interrupted, isImage, noOutputExpected, backgroundTaskId}` on 51.9% of results, that set plus `backgroundCwdHint` on 33.0%, absent entirely on 13.7% (the subagent lane), and may also carry `assistantAutoBackgrounded`, `backgroundEndsWithFinalResponse` or `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`.
claims.depends: csift lifts the task id after the literal `with ID: ` and the output path after `written to: `, falling back to `toolUseResult.backgroundTaskId` / `taskId`; a reworded result string breaks the text path and leaves the id null on the lanes where the structured field is absent.
claims.instrument: Launch any command with `run_in_background` and read the result record: `csift search 'Command running in background' @<session> --raw | head -1`. Counting rule: one verbatim result string per launch; the unit test `helpers_parse_the_result_text_and_locate_the_main_transcript` in src/live/tests/background_scan.rs pins both markers.

claims.behavior: A backgrounded shell's `tool_result` normally arrives sub-second (corpus median 0.42s, 90.4% under 1s) but not always: 9.6% of 2941 pairings took over 1s, 48 took over 5s and the slowest took 197.9s, and 1 launch of 2942 was never paired at all. During that window the launch IS an unreturned call. Once paired - which is the steady state for the whole life of the background command - the tail state machine reports `no pending call`, so a running background shell is invisible to unreturned-call liveness logic.
claims.depends: This is why csift added the whole-file background scan and the seventh verdict `idle-background-open`; before it, a session idling at `end_turn` with a running background build reported `idle-eot` and satisfied `wait --until stop`.
claims.instrument: Launch `sleep 600` with `run_in_background`, then run `csift status @<session>`: the tail row reads `no pending call; last stop_reason end_turn` while the verdict is `idle-background-open` with a shell row. Counting rule: one launch, one status read; the e2e test `an_open_background_shell_is_the_seventh_verdict_with_its_row` in tests/cli/live/background.rs pins it against a fixture.

claims.behavior: An async agent launch is a `tool_result` whose `toolUseResult` is `{isAsync:true, status:"async_launched", agentId, description, resolvedModel?, prompt, outputFile, canReadOutputFile}` (resolvedModel is optional - absent on 36 of 298 corpus acks - and a `modelsUsed` array appears when more than one model was used) and whose text opens `Async agent launched successfully.`, now followed on 66% of corpus acks by a parenthetical warning not to quote the result. The `agentId` is a 17-character `a`-led id and the completion reuses the `<task-notification>` machinery with `<task-id>` equal to it.
claims.depends: csift's launch ingester detects the launch by the sentinel `toolUseResult.status == "async_launched"` (falling back to the text prefix) and lifts `agentId`, `description` and `outputFile` from the structured echo; a renamed sentinel makes async agents invisible to the background section.

claims.behavior: A background task launched from a subagent lane is CLOSED by a carrier in the PARENT main transcript, and the cause is the SINK, not the addressing. The pulse itself is addressed to the launching lane: the backgrounded shell's exit callback fires the completion notifier with the agent id the task was registered under (@164973293), and that notifier addresses its enqueue inline as the owning agent id falling back to the root (@164968716). It never goes through the shared addressing helper, whose call sites are exactly three - the agent-completion enqueuer (@164953647), the workflow notifier (@168826340) and the agent-resume path (@175694140) - beside its definition (@164954861); a whole-binary enumeration of that helper returns those four occurrences and no shell-path use. Nor is a child-addressed pulse absorbed by the main thread: the per-lane fold admits, on the main thread, only items whose agentId equals the root id, and in a child lane only `task-notification` items addressed to that child (@162030912, with the main-thread predicate `agentId === root` at @160411638). So a child-launched shell's pulse can be addressed to that child and never delivered in the main lane at all. What lands in the root file regardless is the QUEUE line: the queue factory builds every queue-operation record with the CURRENT (root) session id and no agentId key (@162031901), the write-policy table gives `queue-operation` the `always` policy while only content-replacement, fork-context-ref and observer-ref are route-by-agent (@166067281), and the store's append defaults its session id to the store's own session and sends an `always` record to that session file (@166106795, routing switch @166107428) - so the enqueue and remove lines are written to the root session file whatever agent the notification was addressed to, and no queue carrier can be diverted into a subagent transcript. Measured 2026-09-03 over the subagent transcripts under the projects root (7,761 at that run): 638 subagent-lane background-shell launches, 633 distinct task ids, 622 closed by at least one carrier in the parent, and ALL 622 carry a queue-operation enqueue line with zero closed without one; an independent run the same day gave 641 launches and 625 closed. Notifications are not strictly absent from subagent transcripts: when the wake router delivers one to an IDLE agent (@179256565) the resume driver mints it in that agent's own transcript as an `isMeta:true` user record (@175692385), and a SECOND child-lane shape exists, a `queued_command` attachment - over those same launches 6 task ids carried the user record and 5 the attachment, so both child-lane counts are floors, not totals (an earlier count on 2026-09-02 recorded 12 isMeta user records in 5 child files, builds 2.1.159 through 2.1.258, under a per-record rather than per-task rule). Every such delivery is also on the parent's queue-operation enqueue and remove line, so a main-only carrier read still sees all of them.
claims.depends: csift reads launches from every lane but carriers only from the main transcript, resolving the main file from a subagent target; scoping the notification index per file instead of per session root inflated never-returned from 24 to 631, a 26x false-positive rate. The main-only carrier read is sound precisely because the closing evidence is the queue line rather than a delivered pulse: a pulse addressed to a child that never wakes still leaves its enqueue and remove lines in the root file, and the fold guarantees the main thread will not absorb it. A child-lane delivery (the isMeta user record, or the queued_command attachment) is therefore an ADDITIONAL shape csift may see, never a closure it would otherwise miss.
claims.instrument: Take a background id launched inside a `subagents/agent-*.jsonl` and `rg -c '<that id>'` in the child file against the parent transcript: the completion appears only in the parent. Counting rule: one launch per (file, tool_use id), `rg -c` counting matching lines; the e2e test `subagent_launches_complete_in_the_parent_main_transcript` in src/live/tests/background_scan.rs pins it.

claims.behavior: A Monitor produces TWO notification shapes, from two different call sites. An EVENT pulse carries only (task-id, summary, event): the monitor's stdout sink is a token bucket (ten tokens, one refilled every 2000 ms) whose data handler calls the event emitter once per admitted line (@163709751), and that emitter builds its notification with a task id, a `Monitor event: "<description>"` summary and an `<event>` body, passing NO status and NO tool-use id (@163710154), so under the shared builder's truthiness rule a pulse cannot carry `<status>` (@162044480). The SAME status-less emitter also writes the housekeeping notices: the arm's timeout callback sends the notice beginning `[Monitor timed out` (@168332544), and the sink sends its own suppression notice and, after 30s of sustained overflow, a stopped-for-too-much-output notice while killing the task (@163709751). A timeout is therefore NOT distinguishable from an ordinary event by tag shape - only by the literal text of the event payload. A TERMINATION notice is the other shape: on shell exit the completion notifier writes (task-id, tool-use-id, output-file, status, summary) with the monitor-specific summary heads `Monitor "..." stream ended`, `... ended without producing output`, `... script failed` and `... stopped` (@164967491). Corpus 2026-09-04, one observation per `<task-notification>` section in a delivered `type:"user"` record whose `<summary>` begins with the word Monitor, over every transcript under the projects root: 1017 sections - 114 termination notices with `<status>` completed in 114 of 114 (no failed or killed termination appears), and 903 status-less pulses, every one carrying an `<event>`, of which 13 are the timeout notice and 890 are ordinary events; no suppression and no stopped-for-output notice appears in this corpus, and no section carries neither a status nor an event. The 2026-09-02 check measured 111 of 111 completed and 841 pulses under the same rule.
claims.depends: csift keeps a monitor OPEN through event pulses (a carrier with no `<status>` and no timeout event leaves the state untouched) and closes it only on the termination notice or a timeout event; treating a pulse as a completion closes a persistent monitor on its first event. Because the timeout notice is shape-identical to an ordinary pulse, csift's close-on-timeout test is necessarily a substring test on the `<event>` payload, which is the only signal available; the sink's two other housekeeping notices ride the same status-less shape and are correctly left non-closing, since the stopped-for-output case also kills the shell and so produces its own status-bearing termination notice. The rendered label likewise falls back to the `<event>` payload instead of fabricating `completed`.
claims.instrument: On a monitor-rich transcript, extract every `<task-notification>` block in `type:"user"` records whose `<summary>` first word is `Monitor` and bucket by presence of `<status>` against `<event>`. Counting rule: one observation per notification BLOCK (a record may hold several), counting only delivered `type:"user"` records so the queue and attachment echoes are not triple-counted; the unit test `a_monitor_is_open_through_event_pulses_until_it_ends_or_times_out` in src/live/tests/background_scan.rs pins the state machine.

claims.behavior: Agent orphans branch three ways - handed to auto-resume, `stopped`, or `failed`. Auto-resume requires FOUR conditions together, not two: an auto-resume callback is present, the agent was launched by the Agent tool or by a forked skill, its meta is fetchable, and its transcript mtime is younger than 172800000 ms (48 hours). Otherwise the split is `stopped` when the transcript mtime is known OR the transcript is fetchable (or the agent was redispatched), and `failed` when neither holds - the harness's own wording for `failed` is that its in-process state was lost. That 48-hour constant is the only aging rule in the whole orphan family (one comparison site; the module carries no other 4+-digit literal).

claims.behavior: Two interrupt bindings share one handler: chat:cancel (escape) always calls pn({gesture:"escape",suppressBackgroundAgentKill:true}), while the global app:interrupt (ctrl_c) handler passes that flag only in the viewing-an-agent branch and otherwise calls pn({gesture:"ctrl_c"}) bare (@180831002). Inside pn the kill routine is reached only under if(!wn&&(_o||ci||h3e())) where wn is suppressBackgroundAgentKill (@180829485), so escape provably cannot kill. The routine filters the task registry by she(T)=fr(T)&&(T.status==="running"||Dm(T))||T.type==="in_process_teammate"&&T.status==="running" - fr is type==="local_agent", Dm is completed-with-pending-work - and no shell, monitor, workflow or remote kind appears in it (@180827798); the constant j4e=3000 declared on the same line is both the double-press chord window and the confirm toast timeout. The routine kills each admitted entry and enqueues the gesture's only on-disk trace, `Background agent "<d>" was stopped by the user.` or `<n> background agents were stopped by the user: ...`, with mode:"task-notification" (@180828701). What the predicate does not settle, and what this claim therefore does not assert: the same branch first calls a wake-registry reset - mz(tt,{durable:false}) (@168768925) opens with p3(),ALe(), where p3 (@163691727) walks every entry of the wake registry clearing its coalesce timer, rescanWanted, pendingConfirm, pendingSeed, idle-rescan cancel and read-retry timer and bumps cancelGeneration, and ALe (@163692217) bumps scanGeneration - so whether an ARMED Monitor still fires after the gesture is not decided by the kill predicate alone. The survival of a backgrounded shell process after an interrupt has never been observed here either; it needs the live trial the instrument names. Corpus 2026-09-04: 10 stopped-by-the-user notices in the whole corpus (9 plural, 1 singular), all classified harness.notification.subagent, none naming a shell or a monitor.
claims.depends: csift's idle-background-open verdict treats an open shell or monitor as still open after an interrupt; assuming the interrupt closed everything produces a false idle-eot, and the resume path starts with an empty in-memory task list so survivors surface only as orphans. The kill predicate backs that reading for shells and monitors to the extent that the kill routine never touches them; it does not license reading an open monitor row as a promise that the monitor will fire again, since the same branch resets the wake registry. csift's row is a report of a launch with no completion carrier, which is exactly what it should stay.

claims.behavior: The task tools persist ONE JSON file per task under a per-list directory at <claude-home>/tasks/<sanitized list id>/<task id>.json (Xk and F @160149333), and TWO directory-name forms exist on real disks because the list id falls through: lA() returns env CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID, else the team name, else the inherited or leader team name, else the session id (@160149333), while session-team init names a team session-<first 8 of the session id> and, when that differs from the session id, RENAMES tasks/<session-uuid> to tasks/<team name> with the rejection swallowed (@183052390) - a best-effort rename, so a uuid-form directory can survive either because team init never ran or because the rename failed, and which cause produced any given survivor is not decidable from the code. The TaskCreate handler writes {subject, description, activeForm, status:"pending", owner: undefined, blocks: [], blockedBy: [], metadata} (@164395722); createTask writes {id: String(highWaterMark+1), ...fields} and updateTask writes {...existing, ...patch, id} through JSON.stringify(...,null,2) (@160151613, @160153498), which is why ids are STRINGS and blocks/blockedBy are always present as lists while activeForm, owner and metadata are optional. The status set is CLOSED, not open: the shipped schema is {id, subject, description, activeForm?, owner?, status, blocks, blockedBy, metadata?} with status the three-value enum ["pending","in_progress","completed"] (@160147000, @160147053), and both readers validate with it and return null after logging "[Tasks] Task <id> failed schema validation" (@160152647, @160153204), so a file carrying a fourth value is dropped by the harness itself. Whether any writer outside this module can land such a value is unread. Corpus 2026-09-04: 184 directories (168 session-form, 16 uuid-form, nothing else), 423 task files; id a string 423/423; blocks and blockedBy lists 423/423; status completed 279, pending 114, in_progress 30 - only the three schema values; activeForm present 337 and absent 86, owner 36, metadata 34; five key sets (271, 82, 34, 32, 4).
claims.depends: csift reads BOTH directory forms and merges them, renders anything that is not `completed` as an open row with its verbatim status (in_progress first, with blockers) and folds completed ones to a count; probing only one form silently reports no tasks for a session using the other, and a numeric-id assumption would drop rows. Rendering the status verbatim rather than through an enum of its own costs nothing today - the harness's reader enforces the same three values - and is what would keep csift honest if a fourth value ever appeared, but it is a csift tolerance choice, not a property of the store.
claims.instrument: `ls ~/.claude/tasks | sed 's/^session-.*/session-form/' | sort | uniq -c` shows both forms; `jq -r .status ~/.claude/tasks/*/*.json | sort | uniq -c` gives the status census; `csift status @<session> --format json | jq '{tasks, tasks_completed}'` prints the rows (null = no dir, [] = a dir with nothing). Counting rule: one row per non-completed task file across both directory forms.

claims.behavior: A background task can be designed never to return (a dev server, a watcher, a persistent monitor), so no completion record will ever arrive for it and `not returned` can never be read as `still running`.

checks.observed: 119070 Bash use/result pairs; 52 disagree (0.0437%), 50 in the top-level lane and 2 in subagent lanes; versions include 2.1.257 (1), 2.1.252 (1), 2.1.251 (11), 2.1.208 (18). Direction, in all 52: the nearest PRECEDING record agrees with the TOOL_USE record (52/52); the nearest FOLLOWING record agrees with the RESULT record in 46/52 and with the tool_use in the remaining 6. So the tool_use record carries the pre-command spawn directory and the result record has already picked up the post-command value.
checks.rule: Disagreeing pairs divided by all Bash tool_use/tool_result pairs joined by tool_use_id, corpus-wide, one comparison per pair; direction decided per disagreement by which side the neighbouring records agree with.
checks.note: The ANCHOR LAW is confirmed correct and still load-bearing, but the rationale printed beside it in src/bash_mutations/cwd.rs 19-21 has the polarity inverted: it is not that the result record lags behind, it is that the result record RUNS AHEAD. The consequence is the same and if anything sharper - anchoring on the result record would join a relative operand against the directory the command left the shell in, i.e. after its own `cd`, which is exactly the wrong directory. The rate is 5.5x lower than the recorded 0.24%: use 0.0437% (about 1 in 2,300). The cited lines exist verbatim; only the wording of the second sentence needs replacing.

producer_chain.name: the shell tool exec loop: the bash_progress emitter
producer_chain.note: The entry. The shell tool runs the command and, on every tick of the running-command generator, hands the consumer a progress record. This is the event that later re-runs the transcript recorder WHILE the command is still running.

producer_chain.name: the pre-poll race: OWn=2000 ms decides whether any progress is emitted
producer_chain.note: A command that finishes inside OWn returns here and emits no progress at all; only a longer command reaches startPolling and the tick above. OWn=2000 is read at 165011157.

producer_chain.name: the tool scheduler drain: getCompletedResults yields pendingProgress
producer_chain.note: Progress messages are handed to the query consumer while the tool status is still executing, i.e. before its result exists.

producer_chain.name: _applyMessage: a bash_progress is applied to the in-memory transcript
producer_chain.note: Vmn(e) is Gts.has(e) and Gts contains bash_progress (166068044), so a shell progress record is dispatched into the transcript as replace-last-ephemeral-progress.

producer_chain.name: the transcript reducer arm returns a NEW array
producer_chain.note: Both exits build a new array (e.with(r,message) or [...e,message]); that array is the recorder effect dependency, so applying a mid-command progress record re-runs the recorder.

producer_chain.name: the message_delta backpatch fills stop_reason on every accumulated assistant record
producer_chain.note: At API turn end every per-block assistant record - including the one carrying the shell tool_use block - stops being stop_reason-null.

producer_chain.note: While a response is in flight the persisted prefix stops at the first assistant record whose stop_reason is still null. Once the backpatch above ran, the tool_use record is no longer withheld, so the next recorder run - the mid-command one - writes it.

producer_chain.name: the REPL recorder record(): the persister
producer_chain.note: The real persister the earlier trace mis-named. It computes the frontier and slices the unpersisted messages; its d5e call is at 181642295.

producer_chain.name: record() hands the released slice to Rw
producer_chain.note: Rw is the append driver; it filters already-persisted uuids and calls insertMessageChain for the rest. This is the call that puts the assistant tool_use record on disk, mid-command.

producer_chain.name: the headless lane persister pu().w(), same frontier, same Rw
producer_chain.note: The non-REPL lane runs the identical frontier and append driver, so the ordering is not REPL-specific.

producer_chain.name: insertMessageChain: the appended entry literal
producer_chain.note: Each entry is built by spreading the message and then the stamper, so the stamper cwd wins and is evaluated per record at append time.

producer_chain.name: Gjt: cwd is a live getter call at append time
producer_chain.note: cwd:ne() - not a value captured at turn start. This is why two records appended either side of the shell mutation carry different directories.

producer_chain.name: the shell read-back continuation: the post-command cwd update
producer_chain.note: Runs inside the tool call on the subprocess result, after the command exits - i.e. AFTER the mid-command append of the tool_use record and BEFORE the result record is built.

claims.behavior: A backgrounded Bash command in which ANY top-level segment's first token is `cd`/`pushd`/`popd`/`chdir` gets the notice `Session cwd remains <path>; directory changes made by the backgrounded command do not apply to subsequent commands.`, carried on `toolUseResult.backgroundCwdHint` and appended to the background block of the result content (measured 1,204 records; 1,204/1,204 match the sentence exactly, appear in the rendered content, and name the carrying record's own cwd).
claims.depends: csift treats a backgrounded command as never advancing the tracked cwd, matching the harness; no csift surface parses the hint, so a rename is not load-bearing, but the underlying suppression is.
claims.instrument: `rg -c 'backgroundCwdHint' ~/.claude/projects --glob '*.jsonl'`; expect a four-digit count in a large corpus. Counting rule: one occurrence per Bash result object carrying the key.

checks.observed: 1204 records carry toolUseResult.backgroundCwdHint. 1204/1204 match the sentence exactly, 1204/1204 also appear inside the rendered tool_result content, and the path in the hint equals the carrying record's own cwd in 1204/1204. Versions include 3 at 2.1.258 and 3 at 2.1.251. Binary: the value is built as `hn=ke.backgroundTaskId&&S9(e.command)?`Session cwd remains ${ne()}; directory changes made by the backgrounded command do not apply to subsequent commands.`:void 0`, appended to the background block (`if(I)_e+="\n"+I`) which is then joined into `[fe,me,_e,j,W].filter(Boolean).join("\n")`. The trigger predicate is `function S9(e){return ep(e).some((n)=>_O(n.trim()))}` over `function _O(e){let n=Uh(uC(e))[0];return n==="cd"||n==="pushd"||n==="popd"||n==="chdir"}`. The tool schema describes the field as "Model-facing note that the session cwd was not changed by a backgrounded command containing a directory-change builtin (cd/pushd/popd/chdir)".
checks.rule: One occurrence per Bash result object carrying the key; sentence match, content presence and path equality each counted per carrying record.
checks.note: Only the trigger wording needed fixing: it is not 'whose text starts with' a directory-change builtin - the command is split into top-level segments and ANY segment whose first token is cd/pushd/popd/chdir arms the hint, so `make build && cd /tmp` in a backgrounded command is enough. The four-digit corpus count the claim predicted is exactly right (1,204). src/bash_mutations/cwd.rs 10-12 exists verbatim.

claims.behavior: A Bash result's `toolUseResult` object carries the always-present key set `{stdout, stderr, interrupted, isImage, noOutputExpected}` (44,340/44,340 objects) plus at least eleven observed optional keys - `backgroundTaskId`, `backgroundCwdHint`, `staleReadFileStateHint`, `gitOperation`, `persistedOutputPath`, `persistedOutputSize`, `returnCodeInterpretation`, `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`, `timedOutAfterMs`, `assistantAutoBackgrounded`, `backgroundEndsWithFinalResponse` (2.1.258 can also emit `backgroundedByUser`, `backgroundedByTurnAbort`, `backgroundedToDeliverMessage`, `ghRateLimitHint`) - and no structured field naming the paths the command touched: the only path-valued key, `persistedOutputPath`, names the externalized stdout file, and modified-file names appear only inside the prose of `staleReadFileStateHint`. The object is absent entirely on 73,006 subagent-lane results and is a bare string on 1,792 error-path results. The rendered result content is assembled as stdout, stderr, the background block, `staleReadFileStateHint` and the rate-limit hint, joined by newlines.
claims.depends: csift keeps `toolUseResult` UNPARSED as a `RawValue` and reads only small named fields through `Record::tur_probe`, so a renamed key silently removes a `recover` freshness boundary or a `search --resolve-persisted` pointer with no error. Because the object names no path, bash file attribution is a lexical parse of `input.command` and is flagged `(heuristic)` on every surface - text, JSON, help and SKILL.

claims.behavior: `toolUseResult` separates `stdout` from `stderr`, and when stderr is empty and no other rendered section is present the tool_result block text equals `stdout` byte-exactly - no wrapper decoration and no line-number gutter (measured 34,246/34,246 such results corpus-wide, 0 exceptions). When stdout is empty the block instead carries the synthetic text `(Bash completed with no output)`. The renderer does apply a leading-blank-line strip and a trailing trim to stdout, which is a no-op on every stored value measured. `cat -n` and `nl` are not absent from real sessions (563 and 96 of 119,190 Bash commands respectively), so a read anchor must gate on the command shape rather than assume no gutter.
claims.depends: csift's `recover` read anchors take a gated command's stdout as the file window verbatim, so a wrapper prefix or a gutter would splice decoration into a reconstructed file; the anchor therefore also demands a non-error, non-interrupted result.

claims.behavior: `toolUseResult.returnCodeInterpretation` is not a generic non-zero marker. Claude Code emits it only for a CLOSED command-to-interpretation table (grep/rg/egrep/fgrep -> 'No matches found', find -> 'Some directories were inaccessible', diff -> 'Files differ', test and [ -> 'Condition is false', plus `git grep`/`git diff` routed to the same two), and only at exit code exactly 1, which that table classifies as NON-error (isError is n>=2). Every other non-zero exit falls to the default interpreter, which marks the call an error and writes no such field. The half that survives is the second: absence does not imply exit zero -- 91 of 91 Bash results flagged is_error:true carried no field. Measured share 30/4599 = 0.65% of Bash results in scope.
claims.depends: csift never infers exit status from the absence of that key; `recover`'s content-anchor gates demand a positively clean result (non-error AND empty stderr) rather than trusting a missing field.

claims.behavior: Claude Code hoists exactly one deterministic bash-danger class - `dangerous-rm`, an `rm`/`rmdir` whose target is a bare `$VAR/...` or `${VAR}/...` - to a human approval prompt EVEN under bypass permissions, as a `classifierApprovable:false` safety check. The transcript keeps only the assistant's unreturned `tool_use` block, and no per-lane control file records the prompt; the ONE disk projection is SESSION-coarse - the top-level session's registry row at `<sessions dir>/<pid>.json`, into which the status patch merges `{status, waitingFor}` while a dialog is open, adding a `statusUpdatedAt` whenever `status` is present (`l$e` at 158821838 forwarding to the pid-file merge `Sn`, which resolves `${process.pid}.json` under the sessions dir and merges the patch into the existing row, at 158820494). `waitingFor` IS persisted while the dialog is up: it is a free-text label from a per-dialog-kind map whose default is the literal `permission prompt` (`fvt(T){return T===void 0?void 0:zS[T]?.waitingFor??"permission prompt"}` at 181515856), and the row reader accepts it verbatim as a string (159697821). It names neither the tool, the tool_use id, nor the lane. So on disk an escalation-blocked lane, a slow tool and a wedged one still share ONE per-lane signature: an assistant `tool_use` block with no `tool_result` for its `tool_use_id`. That block carries exactly FIVE keys, {type, id, name, input, caller}: 223,406 of 223,406 blocks WRITTEN BY THE SHIPPED BINARY carried that key set on 2026-09-03, a block read fresh on 2026-09-04 shows the same five with `caller {"type":"direct"}`, and the only four-key blocks in the whole corpus (137) are records csift's own elicitation sidecar wrote. No permission, escalation, isEscalated or requires_approval field appears on any block; the four-key form {type, id, name, input} is the API WIRE shape, produced by the request normalizer that strips `caller` before sending (`gYn` at 165948669, whose only call site is the request builder). The signature is the UNRETURNED BLOCK, not a stop_reason value: `stop_reason:"tool_use"` is a top-level-lane truth (59,772 of 59,787 records) but holds for only about half of subagent-lane records (85,437 of 163,636; the rest carry a null stop_reason, some with an apiBlockIndex) - both counts 2026-09-03.
claims.depends: csift's lifecycle forces `status:"running"` whenever the newest meaningful record is an unreturned `tool_use` (never `completed`), keying on the UNRETURNED BLOCK rather than on `stop_reason` - which is why it stays correct on subagent lanes, where a null stop_reason is normal mid-message - and it refuses to distinguish slow from wedged. `status`/`wait` read the registry row's `status` field and treat `waiting` as a HITL leg, naming the dialog families it can mean (a question, a permission prompt, a plan approval, a sandbox or worker request) and warning that the row is transition-written so a stale one needs the pid probe to refute it. csift never reads `waitingFor`, and the row is session-coarse in any case, so no lane, tool or tool_use id can be attributed to the pending block: the honest report remains that the pending permission prompt is invisible PER LANE even when the session-level row shows the session is blocked.

claims.behavior: A measured minority of shell calls mutates a persistent file, and an in-place `sed` never yields a deterministic literal-subset content anchor. Rate: 9,996 of 119,110 shell tool_use records (8.39 percent) carried at least one real-path bash mutation row under csift's own classifier on 2026-09-02, counting one record per distinct (transcript, line) carrying a mutation row with a non-null resolution; re-measured on 2026-09-04 the rate is rule-sensitive but stable in kind - 8.51 percent (11,528 of 135,483 blocks) under a strict lexical rule, 12.10 percent (15,886 of 131,238 records) under csift's own classifier when class-marker rows (git:, interp:, pkg:, extract:, fmt:) are counted as mutations too, and 19.99 percent under a generous rule adding package-manager, build and redirection shapes. sed: 292 commands carrying 397 `sed -i` invocations on 2026-09-02, and 251 commands with 318 invocations on 2026-09-04 under a rule counting one invocation per sed occurrence carrying `-i` or `--in-place` (a looser rule that also accepts combined flags and heredoc bodies returns more, so the figure travels with its rule); the fully literal s/OLD/NEW/ pairs, neither side carrying a regex metacharacter, were 55 and 36 respectively. ZERO of them is a content anchor, and the harness makes that structural rather than incidental. At approval time the permission preview rewrites the tool input to carry an internal `_simulatedSedEdit:{filePath,newContent,baseHash}` unless the target is a network path, is not writable, is unreadable because too large, or the edit is too large to preview (176215480); the shell tool's very first statement short-circuits on exactly that field and applies the edit in process (`if(e._simulatedSedEdit&&!n.remoteCall)return Hqo(e._simulatedSedEdit,n,o)` at 165023880); and the applied path returns `{data:{stdout:"",stderr:"",interrupted:!1}}` after a file-history touch, with a sed-shaped stderr on a missing file (165018430). The model-facing schema omits the internal field in BOTH of its branches (the published schema is the internal one with `_simulatedSedEdit` omitted, and `run_in_background` omitted as well where the background form is unavailable, at 165013450), so no model-authored command can carry it and the corpus can never specimen the intercept. Even when the harness itself knows the resulting bytes, the tool_result it writes carries none of them - and a shell-run `sed -i` exits 0 whether or not it matched.
claims.depends: csift's bash content anchors deliberately exclude `sed -i`, `tail`, variable targets and interpreter/ssh heredocs; the anchor classifier admits `sed` only in the windowed-read idiom, so an in-place sed can never reach the anchor path at all. The bash resolution work raised full-target attribution from 27.1 percent to a measured 77.0 percent ceiling; those two attribution figures are the bash-resolution work's own and were not re-measured in this audit.

(1) A READING-TOOL invariant with no Claude Code producer and none possible: csift's label taxonomy is exactly 34 leaf classes (33 at 0.10.0; `harness.meta.system` added in 0.10.1) across three roles - 5 under user, 5 under agent plus 3 under agent.communication, and 21 under harness - and `agent.thinking` is the ONLY leaf whose dotted path is a segment-prefix of another leaf (`agent.thinking.narration`). Re-counted at csift 0.10.3 today from the value-parser error's full dotted paths, bare roles and mid-path prefixes excluded: 34. The count is a property of csift's own enum, so no binary site can ever produce it. (2) What those leaves must COVER, which IS a Claude Code fact: a whole-corpus census on 2026-09-04 over 7,944 transcripts - top-level and subagent alike, workflow journal files and csift's own elicitation sidecars excluded and reported apart - found 1,370,953 non-blank lines, 0 unparseable, 0 without a top-level `type`, and 18 distinct top-level types, of which 133,258 lines (9.72 percent) belong to types no leaf models: the deliberately unpromoted session-state cache lines (last-prompt, permission-mode, mode, ai-title, agent-name) plus six unmodeled types totalling 2,642 lines - atis-latch 1,216, bridge-session 1,148, history-suppression 226, fork-context-ref 33, cost-state 18, continued-in 1. Four of those six carry no uuid and no timestamp and belong with the bookkeeping lines; two carry an instant (history-suppression via `ts`, continued-in via `timestamp`) and are the only leaf candidates. The mapped/unmapped split applies a TYPE-level rule to LINE counts - a type counts mapped when at least one leaf models a record of it - so the 13,830 queue-operation lines ride in the mapped total although only the content-bearing ones classify. The corpus is live: the same census on 2026-09-03 returned the same 18 types over 1,346,372 lines with 132,965 unmapped (9.9 percent), so the totals are dated snapshots while the type SET is stable. On the Claude Code side only one leaf family currently has a connected trigger, gate and writer: harness.notification, from the local background-shell completion handler that mints a background-command pulse (164968441) through the shared pulse builder whose per-tag truthiness loop decides which tags reach disk (162044480) to the user-record constructor whose return literal becomes the line bytes (165936023).

Peer batching: the inbox poller hands every pending message to the peer formatter at once, which wraps each in its own section and joins them with a blank line, prepending the relay preamble ONCE for the whole batch - so one record can hold several inbound peer sections of mixed kind (prose, `idle_notification`, `teammate_terminated`). Notification batching: the wake router groups every queued task-notification for one idle agent and joins their values with a blank line into a single prompt, which the resume driver mints as ONE isMeta user record with the automated-event framing applied once. A whole-corpus census on 2026-09-03 over 7,837 transcripts found 3,794 string-content user records carrying at least one section close and 127 multi-section records: 123 pure peer batches (the largest holding 29 sections) and exactly TWO pure notification batches, of 2 and 3 pulses, both in subagent lanes, each carrying the framing once, 494 characters before the first tag, with pulses separated by exactly one blank line. No record carries a notification section as a SIBLING of a peer section. The two records that hold tags of both families are QUOTING, a third and separate case: a `<task-notification>` tag sits inside a `<teammate-message>` BODY, which the peer writer leaves unescaped because its masking replaces only the section's OWN tag name. The mirror case - a peer tag quoted inside a notification body, which the notification builder appends unmasked - is a PRODUCER fact with ZERO specimens: exactly one `<task-notification>` span in the corpus contains a peer tag, and that span carries no `<result>` element at all.
claims.depends: csift recognizes a section only at a BOUNDARY (content start, immediately after the relay preamble, or right after a prior section's close tag), which is what makes the quoted case safe: a tag inside a section BODY is not at a boundary, so it starts no section and the carrying record keeps its own family. csift scans ALL sections and UNIONs their labels, with notification precedence over a peer tag quoted inside a notification span - a defensive rule that is producer-sourced and still unobserved - mirrors that masking exactly in the per-section text render so classification and render never drift, and emits one hit per section. A plain `contains` check mislabels any genuine message that merely quotes a tag mid-prose, common in csift's own development sessions.

claims.behavior: Optional fields ride the compaction boundary record, and whether isMeta rides it depends on WHICH constructor the lane used, not on what the record means. Both constructors coexist in 2.1.258: the local one (Sce at 166031907) writes isMeta:!1 literally, the stream-event one (Ugt at 163581237) has no isMeta key at all, and the byte writer is JSON.stringify plus a newline, which drops undefined keys - so the key is simply absent rather than false. A corpus census on 2026-09-04 over 235 boundaries: 101 carry an isMeta key and its value is false on 101 of 101, true on 0 of 235; 3 carry agentId and those 3 are exactly the isSidechain:true subagent boundaries (all at version 2.1.219); 1 carries sessionKind with value bg (at 2.1.252), which the envelope builder stamps from the CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KIND env read (158816699) that returns a value only for a background or daemon job. By version, the isMeta-bearing rows are 98 main-thread boundaries stamped 2.1.150 through 2.1.191 plus the 3 subagent rows at 2.1.219, while all 134 isMeta-less rows are stamped 2.1.199 through 2.1.259, 2.1.258 and 2.1.259 included; at 2.1.219 the two lanes disagree in the same build (2 main-lane rows without the key, 3 subagent rows with it). The flip is a ROUTING change, not a constructor change: both constructors coexist from 2.1.191 on, but there the isMeta-less arm is unreachable from an ordinary REPL because no engine ships (tengu_shoji_engine and CLAUDE_CODE_SHOJI_ENGINE have 0 occurrences in 2.1.191, re-measured 2026-09-04), while 2.1.193 is the first shipped build carrying that engine and its gate (env CLAUDE_CODE_SHOJI_ENGINE or the statsig flag, default false, at 212468279) whose boundary arm (215011271) rebuilds the record without isMeta. So 2.1.193 is a CAPABILITY floor with the gate defaulting false into 2.1.199, the observed flip is bracketed by the corpus at 2.1.191 (present) and 2.1.199 (absent), and by 2.1.258 the engine literals are gone from the binary while the isMeta-less stream arm is the live path.

Summaries carry no isMeta key at all (0 of 235; userType external on 235 of 235), so isMeta is an authorship flag on OTHER records rather than something a summary carries. Neither flag reports whether the model received a record. In 2.1.258 the literal occurs 14 times: one constant-table entry, seven write or propagate sites (the two compaction-summary constructions at 164805869 and 164834461, the partial-compaction branch at 164840615, the user-record builder's parameter and object literal at 165935532 and 165936147, and the per-block re-wrap at 165941009 and 165941037) and six readers. Exactly ONE reader is a render filter: hhn (166033049), whose single call site (180551315) applies it as a filter over the transcript view's message list. The other five readers are non-render and none sits on the request path: a backward last-human-turn scan that skips such records (QGr, 162047423), a synthetic-flag helper returning isMeta || isVisibleInTranscriptOnly || isCompactSummary (lwe, 163579507), a submitted-prompt predicate (DV, 165931482), a backward scan that inherits a promptId (ges, literal at 165935121) and the selector search-text extractor (XBt, 180531575). Delivery is carried positively on the other side: the summary is minted with both flags, flattened into the ongoing conversation array by the compaction-result builder (Fne, 164830919) and priced into the boundary's postTokens, and the DAG threads through it - 234 of 235 summary uuids are named as a later record's parentUuid in the same file (children: 214 attachment, 15 user, 7 assistant; 1 summary unthreaded), measured 2026-09-04.
claims.depends: csift keeps the summary LLM-visible (Class::llm_visible excludes CompactionBoundary but not CompactionSummary, src/model/taxonomy.rs) and reads neither flag as a delivery signal; misreading isVisibleInTranscriptOnly as a delivery flag would hide the one record carrying the compacted context from every role-level selector. The instrument must test the PARSED top-level key, never the byte string, or it overcounts several-fold on a corpus whose sessions discuss the field.

producer_chain.note: The byte writer at the end of appendEntry/enqueueWrite: one compact JSON object per line. JSON.stringify silently drops every key whose value is undefined, which is why optional keys are simply absent on disk.

claims.behavior: A compaction summary preserves task STATE in a nine-section synthesis whose section 6 lists the user messages, but it loses user-side TURN fidelity by VOLUME rather than by bullet count: the bullet count tracks the real turn count closely (measured 22 turns to 20 bullets, 27 to 26, 12 to 14 over three sessions), while the bullet text carries only 0.29x to 0.89x the characters of the turns it stands for. Explicit `...`-truncated bullets are the minority form: 67 of 2,089 measured bullets (3.2%), in 38 of 232 summaries. The nine numbered headers are the dominant but not the only rendering - all 232 summaries carry a user-messages section, 165 under the literal header `6. All user messages`.
claims.depends: `verbatim` exists to supplement exactly that loss: it re-emits the clipped verbatim turns in order with their `Lnnnnn` line numbers instead of re-deriving task state, and its dedup fingerprints are extracted from those bullets, so a change to the summary template moves the prefix matching.
claims.instrument: `csift search '' @<session> -t harness.compaction.summary --no-truncate`, count the bullets in the user-messages section, and compare with the genuine-user turn count preceding that boundary (`csift stats @<session> --format json | jq .turns` over the pre-boundary window). Counting rule: summary bullets versus genuine-user turns before the boundary.

Current Work:' and '9. Optional Next Step:'.

Optional Next Step' in 178/232 - the remaining bodies use markdown or unnumbered variants ('All user messages' 52, 'User Messages' 15), while 'Primary Request' and the closing 'Summary:' scaffold appear in 232/232. The 2.1.258 summary shows the full nine numbered sections, 1 Primary Request and Intent through 9 Optional Next Step. Truncation: of 2,089 user-message bullets corpus-wide only 67 (3.2%) end in an ellipsis, and only 38 of 232 summaries contain even one. What is actually lost is character volume, not bullet count: per compaction window, bullets vs genuine-user turns ran 11/8, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 6/8, 13/13, 13/14, 14/12, and total bullet characters vs total turn characters ran 0.89x, 0.38x and 0.29x on the three sessions measured. One session totalled 22 genuine-user turns to 20 bullets, the same shape as the claim's 22-to-17. The binary carries two template variants for section 6, both saying 'List ALL user messages that are not tool results' with no truncation instruction.
checks.rule: Bullets = lines matching a leading '-' or '*' inside the user-messages section of a summary body. Truncated = the bullet's text, with a trailing quote stripped, ends in '...' or a single-character ellipsis. Turns = csift hits labelled user.message whose line number falls strictly between the previous boundary line and this boundary line; characters = length of the untruncated csift excerpt.
checks.note: The claim's direction is right and its 22-to-17 figure is close to a re-measured 22-to-20, but the stated MECHANISM ('clips real prose turns to ...-truncated bullets') is the minority case at 3.2% of bullets. Since verbatim's dedup fingerprints key on those bullets, the correction matters: the bullets are mostly complete quoted messages, which is why prefix fingerprinting works at all. Code verified verbatim at src/turns/build.rs:245-251 and src/turns/config.rs:43-47.

claims.behavior: The assistant side of a compaction summary collapses to AT MOST ONE verbatim quote and often to none: over 8 measured compaction windows holding 785 assistant messages, 3 windows carried exactly one 60-character-verbatim assistant quote and 5 carried zero, and no window carried two. When a quote is present it is not reliably the last pre-compaction assistant message (1 of 3 measured). Every summary ends with a trailer pointing at the full transcript path (232 of 232). CC 2.1.258 ships two section-9 templates and only one of them asks for direct quotes, which is consistent with the quote being optional.
claims.depends: That single end-of-turn quote is why `verbatim`'s agent-message selection defaults to LONGEST rather than LAST and why its richness profiles exist: everything between the first and last assistant message of a compacted turn survives only in the raw transcript.

claims.behavior: A compaction summary is a turn MEMBER, not a turn delimiter, so a backward walk from EOF passes through compaction boundaries transparently. How DEEP the window reaches is budget-relative, and the depth is a measured-at-a-moment figure rather than a constant: at the default 40,000-char budget on the five most compaction-heavy top-level transcripts the crossings were 1/80, 4/33, 5/32, 2/15 and 10/11 on 2026-09-02 and 1/80, 4/33, 3/32, 2/15 and 10/11 on 2026-09-04, the third session having moved because a live session keeps growing above its newest boundary and the budget is then spent higher up. The pattern the tuple illustrates is what is stable: a session whose turns are long spends the budget before the first boundary (1 of 80), a session of short turns crosses nearly all of them (10 of 11, i.e. up to 10 boundaries inside one 40K reconstruction). The two ways of counting agree in every run: the emitted `compaction_boundary` row count equalled the header's `boundaries_spanned` in all five sessions on 2026-09-04 and in all five on 2026-09-02.
claims.depends: `verbatim`'s recency-first selection reaches back across multiple compactions by default (`--max-compactions N` caps the crossing count, demonstrated by the 10/11 session falling to 1 spanned under `--max-compactions 2`) and banners every crossed summary; treating a summary as a delimiter would stop the reconstruction at the newest boundary. Because the crossing depth is budget-relative and moves as a live session grows, no csift surface may treat a particular depth as fixed - the header's `boundaries_spanned` beside `boundaries_total` is the reported pair, and the boundary row's line key is `line`, not `line_no`.
claims.instrument: csift verbatim @<session> --budget 40000 --format json | jq -rc 'select(.kind=="compaction_boundary")|.line' | wc -l, cross-checked against the header row's boundaries_spanned and boundaries_total. Counting rule: boundaries the budget window crossed over the session's total. NOTE the boundary row's line key is `line`, not `line_no` (the row carries exactly kind/line/summary_chars), so the ledger's `.line_no` projection yields null on every row.

claims.behavior: File birthtime is NOT a fork signal. Measured over 64 top-level transcripts, the birthtime is LATER than the first record on 64 of 64 (filesystem copies and migrations move birthtimes past the records; the largest ordinary gap is 45d17h, the median 4h13m). The true fork's gap is only 15h19m and ranks 27th of 64, so any 'first record much older than birthtime' threshold that catches the fork also fires on 26 ordinary transcripts. Comparing a UTC record timestamp against a LOCAL birthtime additionally inflates the delta by the zone offset - the same 15h19m gap reads as 25h19m.

claims.depends: csift's token dedupe takes a per-field MAX across an id's records rather than first-wins (src/stats.rs): identical on clean data, immune to the zeroed replay, and commutative so the rayon fold stays correct; first-wins would make the reported total depend on traversal order, and it breaks in the opposite direction on the other measured shape, a mid-stream partial where output_tokens rises from 2 to 1404 inside one id. The duplicate-uuid replay also means any per-file uuid index must tolerate more than one record per uuid, and a diff between two copies of a record must not treat a parentUuid difference as corruption.

claims.behavior: A compaction does NOT rewrite the transcript: Claude Code APPENDS a `type:"system"` `subtype:"compact_boundary"` record and then, on the VERY NEXT line, a `type:"user"` `isCompactSummary:true` `isVisibleInTranscriptOnly:true` record, so every pre-compaction line number stays valid and the pre-compaction records stay in the same file below the boundary. The boundary is the append point and the summary is always boundary+1 (13 of 13 events measured); the transcript writer is an append call (`appendEntryToFileAsync`), never a rewrite of earlier lines.
claims.depends: The whole `Lnnnn` addressing contract rests on it: `verbatim` reconstructs the clipped turns out of the SAME file (its crossed-summary banner names the summary's own line and says the turns below predate it), a `csift show --line` refetch printed before a compaction still resolves the identical record afterwards, and `image`'s stable id `L<line>i<n>` is stable for exactly this reason. If compaction rewrote or renumbered the file, every stored line address in a prior answer would go stale.
claims.instrument: Note a pre-compaction record's `Lnnnn` from any csift surface, let the session compact, then re-run `csift show @<id> --line <that same line> --format json`: it must return the identical record (same `uuid`). Then `csift search '' @<id> -t harness.compaction.boundary --format json | jq -r '.hits[].line'` must be greater than every pre-compaction line, and the summary's line must be exactly one greater than the boundary's. NOTE the jq path: search JSON nests matches inside `{"hits":[...]}` exchange rows, so a top-level `.line` selects nothing. Counting rule: one boundary record plus one immediately following summary record appended per compaction event; line numbers are 1-based and per file.

Refinements: (a) the ordering is not merely 'summary greater still' -- the summary is exactly boundary+1 in 13 of 13 measured events, and the binary assembles the post-compaction array boundary-first; (b) the claim's instrument line uses `jq -r .line`, which selects nothing against the real envelope (matches live under `.hits[]`); (c) `compactMetadata` in 2.1.258 carries more than the four fields the ledger's prose names -- the constructor writes `{trigger, preTokens, userContext, messagesSummarized}` and `postTokens` is patched in afterwards, and other call sites add `preservedMessages` / `preservedSegment` (with `headUuid`/`anchorUuid`/`tailUuid`), so a consumer must not assume a closed field set. claims.behavior: Claude Code synthesizes the AskUserQuestion tool_result from a ladder over the recorded answers, an optional freeform response and an idle timeout, and that ladder gained a fifth outcome at 2.1.216. In 2.1.215 and below it is FOUR-way: an idle timeout first (the 'No response after Ns ...' text, optionally followed by 'Before going idle the user had selected: <rendered>.'), else a non-blank freeform response ('The user responded: <text>'), else any rendered answer string, UNCONDITIONALLY prefixed 'Your questions have been answered: <rendered>. You can now continue with these answers in mind.', else 'The user did not answer the questions.' From 2.1.216 the answered arm SPLITS on a predicate over every question - no notes recorded AND the recorded answer is one of the offered labels (for a multiSelect question, a non-empty set of offered labels; an unanswered question passes) - keeping the old prefix when the predicate holds and writing 'The user answered: <rendered>. Read the answers carefully - they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed - and follow what they actually say.' otherwise. Measured 2026-09-04: the literal 'The user answered: ' has 0 occurrences in 2.1.215 and 2 in both 2.1.216 and 2.1.258, while the other four templates are present in all three; 2.1.215 and 2.1.216 are adjacent entries in the published version list, so the boundary is as tight as that list allows. The retired phrasing 'User has answered your questions' is absent from 2.1.191 through 2.1.259, so its removal predates this range and cannot be dated here. On disk, a user.answer census on 2026-09-04 returns 100 carriers: 81 lead with 'Your questions have been answered' (record versions 2.1.156 through 2.1.258), 18 with 'The user answered:' (2.1.217 through 2.1.259), and 1 apparent match of the retired phrase that is not an answer at all but a subagent tool_result whose content BEGINS with that phrase as the first row of a marker-count table.
claims.depends: csift recognises an AUQ answer by START-anchored prefix (trim_start plus starts_with) against a LIST of markers, four since v0.10.3: the retired 'User has answered your questions' (kept for historical transcripts), 'Your questions have been answered', 'The user answered:' and the freeform 'The user responded:'. The list is the FALLBACK for records without toolUseResult - the primary boundary signals are a non-empty toolUseResult.answers or, since v0.10.3, a non-blank toolUseResult.response - and 'The user did not answer the questions.' is deliberately excluded because it opens no turn, as is the idle-timeout text. A single hardcoded marker missed the dominant form entirely and silently dropped real user.answer turns, while a contains check false-positived on any tool result that merely QUOTES a marker. The version reading is the practical consequence: a single-prefix list is complete for transcripts written by 2.1.215 and below and lossy from 2.1.216 onward. One measured caveat on the START anchor: it still admits a record whose content OPENS with a marker as quoted text (exactly one such record in the corpus today), so the structured toolUseResult signals must stay primary. All four phrasings are also verifiable synth markers in the search prefilter. The marker list's doc comment in src/model/markers.rs is stale on both counts - it says CC has shipped THREE phrasings and dates 'The user answered:' to 2.1.258, against a four-entry list and a measured 2.1.216 floor.

claims.behavior: A PENDING AskUserQuestion or ExitPlanMode is never flushed to the transcript while it waits: Claude Code buffers the WHOLE assistant turn and commits the `tool_use` to the persisted message array only after the interactive tool resolves (verified across 51 sessions with zero counterexamples; on one measured session the ask's `tool_use` was still absent from disk 37 minutes after its own emit timestamp, and the answering `tool_result` landed about 89 minutes after that timestamp). If such a `tool_use` is on disk, its answer is too - so an option-picker freeze is byte-identical on disk to a stall.
claims.depends: csift cannot render a pending-question state from the native transcript at all; the unanswered window is recoverable only from the hook-written sidecar, whose unresolved pendings `search`/`show`/`verbatim`/`list` merge as if native (a pending marker classifies `agent.tool.use`, renders `(elicitation sidecar)` in place of a line number, and every surface that merged one prints `with elicitation sidecar`). A `status` that inferred 'blocked on a question' from the transcript alone would be fabricating.

claims.behavior: Whether an AskUserQuestion or ExitPlanMode tool_use is on disk while its dialog is open is a TIMING outcome of the persistence frontier - not a question-count rule, and not a change made at 2.1.258. In 2.1.258 the stream loop creates one assistant record per content block, the message_delta event then fills stop_reason on every record of the turn before any tool runs, and the write frontier (166067641: while a response is in flight, stop at the first assistant record whose stop_reason is still null, otherwise the whole array is eligible) therefore releases the ask record the moment the API turn ends; the recorder is an effect whose content dependency is the message-array identity (181643343), so an eligible record reaches disk at the next change of that array, and an in-place field mutation alone schedules nothing. Nothing on that path branches on how many questions an ask carries: the persistence path branches only on stop_reason, on the in-flight flag, on the store array identity and on isLoading, and as supporting evidence the byte substrings 'questions.length' and 'questions?.length' occur 0 times in 2.1.257, 2.1.258 and 2.1.259 while '.questions' occurs exactly 36 times in each, with all 36 in 2.1.258 read and none in the persistence path (that needle set cannot see a count test on a destructured binding - the dialog's own submit path reads such a binding near 181429402 - which is why the negative rests on the read of the write path and the enumeration only supports it). The 2.1.258 boundary is refuted as well: the frontier body is byte-identical in 2.1.257 and 2.1.258 and only minifier-renamed in 2.1.259, and the isResponseInFlight literal enters at 2.1.233 as a recorder-class options-bag rename over an unchanged body, so it dates a refactor. What has actually been measured is a shape, not a rule: in two live trials at 2.1.258 (macOS and a Windows 11 ARM64 guest) an unreturned tool_use whose input.questions held two elements was on disk while the picker sat on question 1, and a single-question ask raised in the same sessions stayed unwritten. The retrospective corpus cannot decide the differential: of 114 AskUserQuestion tool_use blocks readable today, 92 carry one question and 17 carry two to four (spanning record versions 2.1.156 to 2.1.258), ZERO are unreturned (every one of the 137 hits csift labels agent.tool.use for that tool is paired), and the ask/answer order probe leaves 90 of 98 pairs undecidable with every discriminating record a queue-operation line - so no version origin is asserted.
claims.depends: status and wait carry the tail dialog as its own HITL leg beside the registry waiting row and the elicitation sidecar, and the evidence line says which leg fired. The derivation is sound and unchanged: tail_dialog (src/live/verdict.rs 299-302) fires on ANY unreturned AskUserQuestion or ExitPlanMode at the tail and never counts questions, so a pending ask that reached disk is seen without the sidecar while one that did not is still attributed to the sidecar or to the registry row. What is wrong is the JUSTIFICATION csift carries: the comment at src/live/verdict.rs 291-295 and the note emitted under that leg (the string at 347-350) both tell the reader that a multi-question ask is written at question time since CC 2.1.258 while a single-question ask stays buffered - a rule the binary does not implement. The honest wording is that a pending dialog is on disk only when the API turn had already ended and something changed the message array during the wait, so the absence of a tail dialog is never evidence that no dialog is open, and the presence of one is not evidence about how many questions it asks. The claim's code sites need moving too: 170-227 and 255-262 are the pid- and sidecar-evidence blocks and do not hold this claim; the load-bearing site is the tail-dialog block at 291-302.

claims.behavior: The attachment is built by walking the whole read set, skipping any entry recorded with an offset or limit (full-view reads only), requiring the file's mtime to have moved past the recorded read instant, requiring the content hash to differ, and requiring a non-empty rendered diff. The 16 KB budget is the literal constant 16384 and is CUMULATIVE across one batch of attachments: attachments are filled in order until the running total of snippet lengths reaches 16384, after which every remaining snippet is replaced with the empty string. Both tools branch on "no read state OR partial view" BEFORE reaching the mtime comparison and reject from that arm with "File has not been read yet. Read it first before writing to it." A control must be a lone command: the recognizer refuses the whole command string when it contains '|', '<' or '>', so a cat that shares a line with a redirect seeds nothing. Seeding: a lone cat / nl / bat / batcat, or a sed -n 'A,Bp', enters readFileState with the file's content, its mtime as the read timestamp, and (for sed) an offset/limit partial view. Non-invalidation: the seeder's 'if(n.get(C))return' means bash never overwrites an existing entry, and the write side only computes a hint, never deletes state - the one readFileState.delete site found is 'evictRewoundFileTracking', the rewind feature. claims.behavior: `backupTime` records when Claude Code backed the file up, not when the file changed, so it is a bound on the write instant rather than the write instant. The backup never precedes the write (429 of 429 lags non-negative), but the size of the lag depends on which carrier records it: a newly tracked file's first backup rides a `file-history-delta` written at the moment of the write (146 measurements, median 0.25 s, max 3.20 s), while a later bump of an already tracked file waits for the next snapshot (283 measurements, min 29.9 s, median 1,409 s).
claims.depends: csift reports the version transition plus the surrounding INTERVAL rather than an instant, so a consumer never reads the backup time as the write time; presenting `backupTime` as the mutation instant would misdate every silent write.

claims.behavior: The unchanged-file dedup has TWO branches, both gated by one lookup that returns undefined - and so disables both - under the tengu_read_dedup_killswitch gate, on a remote call, or when dedupUnchangedReads===false. Branch A (source:"seeded") fires when the remembered entry is startup-seeded, is NOT a partial view, and the NEW call asks for the whole file (offset===1 and limit===undefined); it compares the file's timestamp for exact equality with the remembered one. Branch B fires when the remembered entry is NOT a partial view AND itself carries a defined offset (i.e. it came from a windowed Read, not from an edit/write-seeded entry), the new call's offset and limit match the remembered ones exactly, and the file's timestamp is exactly equal to the remembered one. Both branches additionally require a pending-handover guard to be false. Because a whole-file Read stores offset===undefined, branch B never dedups a plain whole-file re-read.
claims.depends: The `!isPartialView` precondition is why a token-cap-truncated read is always re-read in full later, which is the only reason csift's contentless `file_unchanged` handling has not yet produced a wrong recovery.

claims.behavior: Claude Code writes the model-facing image handle into the carrying record's own text as the literal marker `[Image #N]`, one marker per pasted image, and echoes the same handles as that record's `imagePasteIds` array. The marker is minted and inserted at PASTE time, not at submit: the image-paste keybinding hands the clipboard image to the paste callback (2.1.258 @181174777), whose image branch mints an id, stores the entry under it, and appends the template to the input text (@181171669), the template being the one-line function that returns `[Image #<id>]` (@162013342). At submit the record builder writes the submitted text block first and the image blocks after it on ONE user record, with the same ids in `imagePasteIds` (@169779566). Marker ORDER is not guaranteed to match block order: the block array and `imagePasteIds` are built in a single pass over the paste store's values, which is ascending by numeric id (@169787110), while the markers sit wherever the operator's editing left them in the input text, so the two orders can diverge. Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one observation per user record with a non-empty `imagePasteIds`: 659 records, 639 with the marker count equal to the image-block count AND the marker order equal to `imagePasteIds`, 18 with the same numbers in a DIFFERENT order (markers 179,181,180 against ids 179,180,181; markers 33-41,43,42 against ids 33-43; markers 3,4,9,2,19,22,23 against ids 2,3,4,9,19,22,23; markers 108,107 against ids 107,108), and 2 with mismatched counts. The harness's own reader is number-keyed, never positional: the inverse parser sitting immediately after the template maps each match to {id: parseInt(...)} (@162013342). A handle is unique within one prompt, but the counter does NOT restart at #1 on every prompt: the allocator starts at next = 1, mint() only ever does next++, and the advance helper raises next and never lowers it (@162027126), so within one process handles climb monotonically - measured across one transcript the distinct handles climb 1..624 over many prompts (2026-09-02) - and a fresh process starts at 1 again, which is what makes a handle non-unique within a transcript (IMG-006).
claims.depends: csift recovers `#N` by positionally zipping a record's `[Image #N]` markers with its image blocks and leaves the number unset only when the two COUNTS differ (src/image/refs.rs 275-282). Because count agreement does not imply order agreement, that zip MISASSIGNS the handle on every order-divergent record - 18 of 659 in the corpus today - and the count-mismatch guard does not fire on any of them, so the wrong `#N` is emitted silently. The sound join is by NUMBER: match each `[Image #N]` marker against the record's own `imagePasteIds`, which is what the harness's own parser does. Addressing itself is unaffected either way, since it falls back to the always-unique `L<line>i<n>` locator; and a change to the marker format would still lose the model-facing handle entirely.

claims.behavior: A transcript's [Image #N] handles are neither dense nor anchored at #1: the number comes from one per-session counter that is only ever raised, and a handle reaches a record only if its marker survives to submit. Re-measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root: 177 files carry [Image #N] handles; 100 of them start above #1 (9 of those top-level); 77 carry at least one hole inside their own [min, max] - the largest top-level file holds 575 distinct handles over #1..#624 with 49 holes, the next 120 over #1..#131 with 11 holes. The counter produces both shapes. The allocator returns next++ and never reissues or lowers a number, its advancePast only raises it, and startEpoch resets the minted set and never the counter (byte 162027126); on resume every handle in the LOADED history raises next before the session mints anything (byte 162027795), which is why a continued history starts above #1 - in the one top-level transcript headed by a compact_boundary the highest inherited marker is 619 and the first minted imagePasteIds are [620, 621] (re-checked 2026-09-04). The holes have named causes rather than 'inherited from paste time': one counter serves both marker templates, which sit side by side ([Pasted text #N] and [Image #N], byte 162013247); a large TEXT paste mints a number (byte 181170595 - only a paste over the size or line threshold mints, a small one is inserted verbatim) whose marker is replaced by the pasted content at submit and so never reaches a record (byte 162014339); and an image paste whose marker leaves the input before submit is deleted from the draft store with its number already spent (byte 170594396). claims.behavior: One pasted image can appear as several separate image blocks inside one transcript, and the traced cause is a RECALLED OR EDITED DRAFT resent under its existing paste ids. In 2.1.258 the path is: a turn-end user-cancel with an empty input restores the last user record into the draft (byte 181627085), and the explicit restore entry reaches the same function through setImmediate (byte 180779402); restoreMessageSync filters that record's image blocks out of its content and puts them back into the draft store keyed by the record's own imagePasteIds (byte 180778472); the paste-id helper keeps an id already minted this epoch instead of issuing a new one (its allowCurrentEpochSkip branch, byte 162029083), and the queued-message path re-adds queued images under their existing ids (byte 181689815); on the next submit the draft's image pastes are turned back into blocks and ids (byte 169786520) which the record builder writes, together with imagePasteIds, onto a NEW user record (byte 169779530). Neither cause this claim used to state survives its gates. There is no surviving store to re-send from: the draft's clear empties the whole paste map (byte 180837212), the submit handler calls it on every non-keybinding submit (bytes 181685480 and 181685514), the queue branch clears independently (byte 181580116), an input-change subscriber deletes every image paste whose marker has left the text (byte 181169506), and the submit chain forwards only pastes whose marker is still in the submitted text (byte 181576900). claims.behavior: Claude Code ships an atomic-write helper that writes through a temporary file and a rename, plus a documented non-atomic fallback whose error is prefixed `atomic write failed first: `. Both paths are present in the shipped binary. But the binary DOES attribute one of the four JSON sidecars a reader joins: the session-registry row `<claude-home>/sessions/<pid>.json` is written with plain `fs/promises.writeFile` on both its registration and its update path (and the sibling `.fleetview-heartbeat` likewise), NOT through the atomic helper - the writing module's own import header binds `writeFile as Mg` alongside the `join` and `readFile` aliases that same function uses. A plain writeFile truncates in place, so the registry row is not merely 'to be assumed' observable half-written: it is positively established as such, and csift's skip-on-unparseable guard is required rather than merely prudent. The other three sidecars - subagent `meta.json`, workflow run manifests, harness task files - remain unattributed by this instrument; a serialized write chain (`pidFileWriteChain`) orders the registry row's writers against each other but does nothing for a concurrent external reader.
claims.depends: csift reads all four sidecars as a whole-file read plus a parse and silently skips a file that fails either step, so one caught mid-write yields a DOWNGRADED answer with no disclosure: `status` falls back to its no-registry lane, a task row disappears from the tasks section, and a subagent loses its type and its teammate discrimination. Retrying the read once, or disclosing the skip as evidence, is the only way that failure could become visible.
claims.instrument: `strings -n 40` over the installed Claude Code binary grepped for `atomic write failed first` shows the helper (temp file, symlink-refusing O_EXCL open, fsync, rename) and its in-place fallback; `strings -n 12 <binary> | grep -oE 'appendFileSync|renameSync|mkdtempSync' | sort | uniq -c` gives 24 / 15 / 11 and bounds call sites from above without attributing any. To ATTRIBUTE a sidecar, do not count - resolve the alias: find the writer by a literal only it contains (for the registry row, ``Ct(e1(),`${process.pid}.json`)``), then find the nearest preceding `import{...}from"fs/promises"` header in the same module text and require that every identifier the writer calls is bound there. The registry row resolves to plain `writeFile`. claims.behavior: A MAIN transcript GROWS while its session is idle - queue enqueues, `attachment` records and metadata lines are appended with no model turn - so file mtime or byte growth alone is never evidence of activity.
claims.depends: csift classifies WHAT landed rather than whether the file moved: `tail_shape` reads record shape and ignores mtime, and `wait` folds each newly appended record through `classify` instead of treating growth as an event; an mtime-based liveness heuristic would call every idle main session running.

code.snippet:
//! F9: growth alone is never activity - a main transcript grows while idle (enqueues,
//! attachments). This module classifies WHAT the tail is, not whether the file moved.

claims.instrument: Leave a session idle and enqueue a message, or let another session's background task complete into it: the file grows (`stat` mtime and byte length advance) while `csift status @<session> --format json | jq .verdict` stays idle. Counting rule: compare the byte delta over a fixed idle interval against the verdict, then `csift search '' @<session> --turn -1 --count-by label` to show no new agent records.

claims.behavior: A completion pulse is addressed by OWNER LIVENESS, not by lane class. The enqueuer computes the destination through one selector that returns the OWNER AGENT's lane while that owner task is registered and running (or backgrounded with live children) and the root lane otherwise (byte 164954861), and the per-lane queue fold admits, inside a child, exactly the task-notification items addressed to that child (byte 162030912) - so a child branch exists by construction. On the main lane the queued item becomes a prompt record through the REPL drain (byte 181584368); on a child lane the wake router resumes the addressed agent with the pulse as its prompt (byte 179256653), the record is built isMeta with origin task-notification (byte 175692385), and the runner appends only that new record to the lane file (byte 163784699). A delivered child pulse does NOT open with the raw tag: the task-notification case wraps the text with the [SYSTEM NOTIFICATION - NOT USER INPUT] preamble (bytes 166046409, 160018067), leaving the tag about 494 characters in. Main-only delivery is therefore a corpus OUTCOME - owners are usually gone by delivery time - and not a rule: re-measured 2026-09-04 over 8,084 transcripts, 2,885 delivered pulses open in the raw-tag form across 25 main transcripts, while 4 subagent lanes carry 9 preamble-form deliveries, each isMeta true, isSidechain true, origin kind task-notification, tag at index 494 - 8 written by build 2.1.252 and 1 by the audited 2.1.258. (Other carriers of the same tag, counted separately and excluded: 8,270 queue-operation lines, 4,780 attachments, 1,650 non-opening user records, 737 assistant prose.)
claims.depends: csift's child-lane state machine may legitimately use recency (the generating state) while the main-lane verdict never does - but the reason is not that a child transcript grows only from its own message flow: a child lane can gain a record it did not write when a completion pulse is delivered to it, and because that delivery RESUMES the lane, recency still tracks liveness there. Any counting rule, in csift or in this ledger, that looks for a delivered pulse must not test for a raw <task-notification> opener, since a child delivery arrives behind the [SYSTEM NOTIFICATION - NOT USER INPUT] preamble; the main-lane trap that keeps recency out of the main verdict is unchanged.
claims.instrument: While a subagent runs, watch both files: `csift status @<session> --format json | jq '.children[] | {session_id, state, detail}'` reports the child by its own tail age, and the main file receives the `<task-notification>` the child file never carries. Counting rule: notification records per file, main versus each subagent transcript.
