writer_literal_floor.ladder: every eighth build 2.1.150..2.1.259 plus 46 cached builds; a literal dates itself, not the behavior

claims.behavior: Each workflow run's `journal.jsonl` (one per `wf_*` directory) is written INCREMENTALLY - `{type:"started", agentId}` at spawn and `{type:"result", agentId, result}` at return - so for a RUNNING run `started` minus `result` is the number of that run's agents in flight (measured live: 57 started, 49 returned, 8 in flight). It is not a liveness test on its own: a killed, failed or abandoned agent never writes a `result`, so the imbalance is permanent - 613 of the 621 unbalanced entries in this corpus belong to journals untouched for 15 h to 77 days. The journal also carries a third type, `failed`, which is neither counted.
claims.depends: csift's `children_report` sums that difference across a session's journals as `journal_in_flight`; an imbalance is a LIVE signal precisely because a terminal dump would always balance.

code.snippet:
// Workflow journals: started - result per wf dir (incremental, so an imbalance is a
    // LIVE signal - a terminal dump would always balance).

claims.instrument: `rg -o '"type":"(started|result)"' <a wf_*/journal.jsonl> | sort | uniq -c`. Counting rule: one event per journal line, per type; started minus result equals the agents in flight for that run.

checks.instrument: `find ~/.claude/projects -path '*/subagents/workflows/*' -name journal.jsonl -print0 | xargs -0 cat` piped to a python type/key-set census; then per journal `rg -c '"type":"started"'` minus `rg -c '"type":"result"'` paired with `stat -f %m` age; then `csift status @<8-char prefix of a long-idle session> --format json`; then the file listing of the one workflow directory whose journal was written in the last hour.
checks.observed: 160 journals, 12,754 lines: `started` 6,687, `result` 6,066, `failed` 1. Exactly two key sets: {agentId, key, type} 6,688 and {agentId, key, result, type} 6,066. Corpus-wide started minus result = 621. 124 journals balance at 0; 36 carry a positive imbalance, and 35 of those 36 - 613 of the 621 - were last written 15 h to 1,843 h ago (77 days). `csift status` on a session whose tail record is 58 d 19 h old prints evidence `children: 3513 lane(s), 359 live (359 workflow agent(s) in flight)` and verdict `waiting-children`. The single journal written within the hour, belonging to a run that was actually executing, reads started 57 / result 49.
checks.rule: One event per journal line, per `type`; started minus result per journal directory. A journal counts as stale when its file mtime is more than 1 h old.
checks.note: The mechanism holds and was confirmed live, but the inference 'an imbalance is a LIVE signal precisely because a terminal dump would always balance' is refuted: 98.7% of the corpus-wide imbalance sits in long-dead runs. The consequence is a live csift defect, reproducible in one command - `csift status` on a session whose newest record is 58 days old reports 359 workflow agents in flight and returns the verdict `waiting-children`. src/live/children.rs:104-105 and 126-130 match verbatim; the `_ => {}` arm at 129 is what drops the `failed` type, so a failed agent inflates `journal_in_flight` by one forever. A fix would need to age the journal (or its run) the way child lanes are aged, and to count `failed` as terminal.

claims.behavior: Claude Code appends whole LINES to a transcript through a single path, so complete-line framing is the guard a reader needs. The write queue turns each entry into one JSON-serialized line, accumulates lines into a chunk with a 100 MiB ceiling (MAX_CHUNK_BYTES 104857600) on a 100 ms flush timer (byte 166082942), and hands each chunk to appendToFile, which calls the one append helper with THREE arguments (byte 166085326) - so the helper's onlyIfExists parameter is undefined on this path and the ordinary append is either the storage backend's own append or a single appendFile(path, chunk, {mode:0600}) with a mkdir-and-retry fallback (byte 166117719, the direct arm at 166118675). A record larger than the chunk ceiling is not split by the harness: the drain flushes what it has and the oversized entry gets a chunk of its own, still one append call. The foreign-transcript appender, which writes in an explicit loop and can report a torn result (byte 166118748), is reached only under onlyIfExists, whose three producers in this build all target ANOTHER session's file. Claude Code models a torn tail rather than assuming it away: while a seal is pending the next append is prefixed with a newline (the head of the append helper), and a synchronous sealer opens the file write-only and append-only and writes a bare newline when the file is non-empty (byte 166084862) - so a torn line is fenced off, not completed. Measured (2026-09-02): no transcript was left with an unterminated final line (0 of 430 files) and no line was left unparseable (0 malformed in 20,677 lines censused by csift stats). A partially written final line is possible rather than routine - the longest single line was 2,609,260 bytes and 142 lines exceeded 64 KiB - but it was never caught: 0 torn tails in 18,238,418 samples covering 190 observed appends.
claims.depends: csift's tail reader and wait's incremental cursor both stop at the last newline and hold the torn remainder for the next poll; parsing the torn line would surface a spurious malformed-line count on every live read. The writer's own seal is a second reason to hold rather than to guess: a sealed tail is terminated by the newline the writer prepends to its next append, so the held remainder becomes a complete but truncated line, which csift's malformed-line accounting would then count out loud rather than hide - the honest outcome, and one no observation in this corpus has produced.

claims.behavior: The shared <session-uuid>/ directory beside a transcript is minted LAZILY by the first write under it - in practice the first subagent lane append - and not by any elicitation. The path resolver keeps a top-level session transcript FLAT and puts only lanes, journals and session journals under <sessionId>/ (byte 157719971), so nothing addresses the directory until one of those is written; a lane write reaches it through the sidechain record path (bytes 166114240 and 166107661: a sidechain record carrying an agentId is enqueued against the lane path); and the directory is created only as a side effect of the append failing - the direct appendFile arm's catch does a recursive mkdir at mode 0700 and retries (byte 166118593; when the storage pin routes the append through the backend arm instead, that catch is not the arm that runs). Corpus consequence, re-measured 2026-09-04: 64 session directories, 27 of them holding subagents/, 20 holding the elicitation sidecar file; of those 20, 13 sit in a directory older than the file by more than 1 s (min 183 s, median 118,410 s or about 1.4 days, max 775,906 s or about 9 days) and 11 of those 13 also hold subagents/, while 7 have a directory born with the file. The sidecar FILE itself is not a Claude Code behavior at all: the shipped binary contains zero occurrences of the sidecar filename and zero of either marker field (re-confirmed on 2.1.258), because a recording hook writes that file.
claims.depends: csift wait re-attempts sidecar path resolution on every poll instead of resolving once at start, and joins the file at offset 0 when it appears (wholly post-start by construction); a one-shot resolution would miss every elicitation that began after the watch, which is exactly the class of event a wait exists to catch. The directory may already exist when the watch starts - any session that has spawned a subagent has one - or may be born mid-wait, and csift resolves the path on dir.is_dir() alone, so the path can resolve long before any ask has occurred, at which point the sidecar file simply does not exist yet: absence at start is the normal state and never an error.

claims.behavior: A transcript is normally EXTENDED by appends, but appends are not the only thing that reaches the file: one write queue and one 100 ms flush timer carry three item kinds, and two of them mutate a transcript in place (byte 166086064, the drain's item routing - only the third arm is an append). One in-place path is gated off: the compaction rewrite runs only when the store's local GC flag is set, and its class default is false (bytes 166084451, 166076591). The other is NOT gated: a tombstone removal opens the transcript r+, truncates it at the removed record's line and rewrites the tail (byte 166095481, which carries no flag test, and byte 166096106), its live entry is an ordinary REPL stream handler (byte 181621337), and the selecting condition fires the disk removal exactly when the tombstoned record's index sits BELOW the append frontier - that is, when the record is already on disk (byte 179092573). A live transcript can therefore shrink in place, and a byte-offset cursor can outlive the bytes it named. What does hold is the other half of the old sentence: the harness offers a watcher no event stream at all, only the file, so content already on disk before a watcher's snapshot is never re-emitted to it - the append arm writes only at the end of the file, with no seek and no rewrite (byte 166118593), and a 150 s sampler over 33 actively written transcripts (495 observations, 2026-09-03) saw 122 growths, 0 shrinks and 0 changes to any byte below the first snapshot's length, a growth-only window that cannot stand in for the missing gate.
claims.depends: csift seeds a byte-offset baseline per watched file at start and prints a readiness line on stderr so a scripted caller can order its own trigger AFTER the snapshot; without that line an append racing the snapshot is correctly treated as history and the wait hangs to its timeout. That baseline is exact against growth and NOT against an in-place removal below the cursor: the poll skips any file whose length is at or below its stored offset (src/live/wait.rs), so a truncation stalls the watch until the file grows back past the stale offset and the resumed read starts mid-line. No csift surface detects that shrink today.

claims.behavior: The shipped binary's process start-time guard degrades to a PASS when its probe returns nothing. One probe is one shelled command, LC_ALL=C TZ=UTC ps -o lstart= -p <pid> with a 1 s timeout, returning the trimmed stdout or undefined on any failure or empty output (byte 158134674; an async twin at byte 158136222 has the same shape behind a cache that records a miss but never substitutes a value). Both guard forms then read a missing token as a MATCH - the guard returns true when the stored token is undefined, and the comparator returns true when either side is undefined (bytes 158134798 and 158134903) - so a pid whose start time cannot be read is treated as the same process rather than failing closed, and a consumer such as the delayed SIGKILL proceeds on that reading (byte 158133164). No in-process liveness probe substitutes for it, and that is an enumeration rather than an assumption: the same module exports a kill(pid,0) probe, a /proc/<pid>/stat reader, an ESRCH form and a /proc entry counter, and composes them elsewhere into a layered dead_pid | procstart_mismatch | zombie | live verdict, but none of the four is consulted on the start-time path. The environment fact that motivates the guard - a minimal (busybox) userland's ps rejects the -p flag and does not know lstart, so the probe fails even for a LIVE pid, while /proc/<pid> answers liveness directly on Linux and does not exist on macOS - is produced by the operating system's own process lister rather than by this binary, and belongs in its own specimen-only entry.
claims.depends: csift makes the same degradation VISIBLE instead of silent: its probe treats a failing or empty ps as no-verdict rather than dead, falls back to a /proc/<pid> directory test before declaring a pid dead, and when either side's procStart is missing or unparseable it reports the process alive with the reuse guard marked skipped and says so in the evidence (src/live/registry.rs) - a wrong Dead here turns every verdict into stale-dead. The binary's tolerance is why the fallback has to exist, and the disclosure is what separates csift's reading from the binary's silent pass.
claims.instrument: Run `ps -p $$ -o lstart=` on a busybox userland (empty output, non-zero status) versus on macOS or glibc Linux (a local-zone date). Counting rule: one probe per platform. The unit tests `probe_pid_own_process_guard_states` and `probe_pid_reports_a_reaped_pid_dead` in src/live/tests/surfaces.rs pin the alive and dead arms; only a real run on a busybox host can confirm the fallback path.

claims.behavior: `ps -o lstart=` renders its date in at least two field orders - `Sun Aug 16 09:04:23 2026` and `Sun 16 Aug 09:04:23 2026` - and the order is chosen by the LC_TIME locale of the process that runs ps, not by the host family: one macOS host produced the first order under LC_ALL=C and en_US.UTF-8 and the second under en_GB.UTF-8 and en_AU.UTF-8. Claude Code avoids the ambiguity for its own registry field by pinning the environment (`LC_ALL=C TZ=UTC ps -o lstart= -p <pid>`), so procStart is always the C-locale order in UTC; a probe that inherits the caller's locale, as csift's does, sees whichever order that locale selects.
claims.depends: csift tries both strftime patterns before giving up and degrading to a disclosed pid-only probe; matching only one order silently disables the pid-reuse guard on the other family of hosts.
claims.instrument: `for L in C en_US.UTF-8 en_GB.UTF-8 en_AU.UTF-8; do LC_ALL=$L ps -p <pid> -o lstart=; done` on a single host, then the same four locales around `csift status @<id> --format json | jq '.evidence[]|select(.surface=="pid").value'`. Counting rule: one rendering per locale; every order must yield `alive (start-time guard matched)`, because a strftime parse that falls through both patterns degrades to `alive (pid only)` and silently disables the pid-reuse guard.

All 24 subagent records sit under a SINGLE parent session and all carry client version 2.1.251; that session has 15 subagent lanes on one model id and only 5 of them carry any narration (per file 1/2/2/6/13), four with bare-hex subagent ids and one with a name-embedded teammate id. Nothing in the shipped binary decides whether a returned block is tagged: the tag bytes are copied verbatim off the stream (Hs.signature=Cu.signature, 165442020) and the only narration-aware client branch is a memoized read-only predicate (176601820) whose consumers touch no persistence, so the rate has no producer here and stays a measured base rate over a dated corpus. A lane-shaped thinking gate does exist, but on the REQUEST side and not over block tags: the subagent lane runner builds the child lane's config through sor (163781898 -> 158520661), which forces display:omitted for a synchronous, non-forwarding, non-exact-tools child lane and returns the parent config unchanged whenever the session is interactive; the value it may rewrite comes from the showThinkingSummaries setting through mEt/rAn (158520075), the settings schema declares that display as exactly summarized|omitted on both thinking-config variants (158538648), and it reaches the wire as the request's thinking parameter (165412140, spread into the request body at 165415790). Whether display=summarized is what makes a returned block carry the tag is decided upstream of this binary, and which display each lane actually requested is unrecoverable from disk: a byte census on 2026-09-03 found 0 records carrying a structured display, thinkingConfig or interactivity field (the bare tokens occur only as prose inside sessions that discuss them).

checks.note:
REFUTED, and the refutation is triple-instrumented. Claude Code does write narration-tagged thinking blocks into subagent transcripts: 24 of them sit in 5 subagent transcripts of the live corpus, and the spanned-versus-restricted census that the claim cites as proof of equality now differs by exactly that 24 (3103 vs 3079). The blocks are genuine, not a csift artifact - a protobuf decoder written independently of csift finds the same 24 signatures tagged 'narration' in the same five files, and a raw byte grep for the three base64 alignments of the tag returns the same 2/2/6/1/13 per-file split.

New behavior as measured: narration in subagent lanes is real but sporadic and bursty. It is concentrated - all 5 carrying transcripts belong to ONE parent session, while 10 sibling subagent transcripts of that same session, running the same single model id, carry only 'thinking'-tagged signatures. So it is not gated on the subagent lane and not gated on the model; within one session some subagent turns get a narration block and others do not. Both on-disk shapes are represented: four bare built-in subagent transcripts and one name-embedded teammate transcript. Base rates for a stranger: 24 narration records across ~7.5k subagent transcripts (5 transcripts, 0.07% of files) versus 3079 across 66 top-level transcripts (22 transcripts, 33% of files) - three orders of magnitude rarer per file, which is a plausible reason the original scan read as a clean zero.

Honesty about WHY it drifted: every one of the 24 records carries client version 2.1.251, not 2.1.258, and all five files were fully written on 2026-09-01 - the same date the claim records as its measurement. So these records were already on disk when the claim was made, and this is most likely a scope gap in the original measurement rather than a behavior change between 2.1.251 and 2.1.258. Either reading leaves the claim's assertion false against the current corpus, which is why the verdict is drifted rather than refined: the claim's entire content is an absence, and the absence does not hold.

What survives intact is the claim's 'depends' clause, and it is now positively demonstrated rather than merely argued: csift runs the identical signature classifier on subagent files, so the subagent narration was counted with no code change - src/stats.rs:289-291 is unmoved and its counter reports 30 blocks spanned vs 6 restricted on the affected session. The ledger entry should be rewritten from an absence claim into a rarity claim with the per-file base rates above.

claims.behavior: Claude Code derives the `<ENCODED>` project-directory basename from the session's canonical start cwd by NFC-normalizing it and replacing every UTF-16 CODE UNIT outside [A-Za-z0-9] with exactly one `-`, position-preserving: no collapsing of consecutive dashes and no case folding, so `.`, `/`, `_` and space each become one dash, an NFD-spelled accent recomposes to a single unit (one dash), and an astral character (two surrogate units) yields TWO dashes. Since 2.1.234 this is the DEFAULT rather than the only path: the basename is `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME ?? sanitize(cwd)`, and the override is honored only when `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is also set and the value matches /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/ and is not a Windows reserved device name.
claims.depends: `path::encode_cwd` reproduces the transform unit-wise to locate the project directory; a char-wise or byte-wise replacement diverges on any non-ASCII cwd, so every subcommand that takes a real path or `.` as its target silently scans the wrong project or none.
claims.instrument: Pick any directory under `~/.claude/projects/`, read the `cwd` of the first record of one contained `*.jsonl` (`head -1 <file> | jq -r .cwd`) and apply the transform by hand: the result must equal the directory basename character for character. Counting rule: one output dash per UTF-16 code unit that is not ASCII-alphanumeric, so an astral character contributes two dashes and an NFC-composed accent one. The unit test `encode_matches_cc_exactly_on_non_ascii_and_windows_paths` pins NFC/NFD parity, the astral double dash and the Windows shape; to re-derive from the harness, run `strings` over the shipped Claude Code binary and grep for the literal replacement regex `[^a-zA-Z0-9]` and for `normalize("NFC")`, expecting one sanitizer and no case fold.

claims.behavior: Because the sanitizer does no slash, colon or case pre-processing, a Windows cwd encodes to a LETTER-led directory name - `C:\Users\x` becomes `C--Users-x` (the drive letter passes through, the `:` and each `\` are one unit each) - while a UNC root `\\server\share` becomes the double-dash-led `--server-share`; a Unix cwd is always single-dash-led.
claims.depends: csift's `@`-token grammar admits both encoded shapes: a leading `-` token and the `<letter>--...` drive shape are project-dir tokens (a drive-shaped token that matches no directory falls through to real-path resolution, since it can also be a relative path), and a UNC-encoded directory is targeted as `@--server-...` because a bare `--`-leading token is reserved for the mistyped-flag guard; without the drive-shape arm a Windows project directory is unreachable.

#[test]
fn encoded_token_shapes_unix_windows_unc() {
    assert!(looks_like_encoded_token("-Users-dev-example-project"));
    assert!(looks_like_encoded_token("C--Users-dev-proj")); // Windows drive shape
    assert!(looks_like_encoded_token("--server-share-proj")); // UNC (leads with --)
    assert!(!looks_like_encoded_token("Users-dev")); // no encoded lead-in
    assert!(!looks_like_encoded_token("C--Users/dev")); // a separator disqualifies
    assert!(!looks_like_encoded_token("C-Users-dev")); // one dash after the drive ≠ `C:\`

claims.behavior: An EMPTY-STRING `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is still taken as SET by Claude Code, because the null-coalescing operator guarding the read tests only for null/undefined - so the harness resolves its config home to the empty string rather than falling back to the OS home, and every path derived from it becomes RELATIVE to the process cwd (a one-shot run in an empty directory mints `projects/`, `sessions/` and `backups/` there, transcript included). The coalescing read is NOT the only way the harness reads this variable: the global `.claude.json` path and the runner config path read it with a truthiness fallback instead, so an empty value falls back to the OS home on those sites and the harness ends up split between two roots in one process.
claims.depends: csift treats an empty `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` as UNSET and falls through to the OS home's `.claude` - a deliberate, documented divergence (honoring the empty value would resolve the projects root to the relative path `projects`, i.e. whatever happens to sit under the invoking cwd, and normally a hard `cannot read projects root` error rather than the corpus); the same non-empty test also gates the lazy home lookup, so a relocated root still works when `$HOME` is unset.

python3 - <<'EOF'  (whole-corpus, one pass)
import os,re,json,glob
root=os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/projects")
pat=re.compile(rb'"sessionId"\s*:\s*"([^"]*)"')
for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(root,"*","*.jsonl"))):
    base=os.path.basename(f)[:-6]; vals=set()
    for raw in open(f,"rb"):
        c=pat.findall(raw)
        if not c: continue
        s={x.decode("utf-8","replace") for x in c}
        if s=={base}: vals.add(base); continue
        try: o=json.loads(raw)
        except Exception: continue
        if isinstance(o,dict) and isinstance(o.get("sessionId"),str): vals.add(o["sessionId"])
    # tally: base not in vals -> mismatch; len(vals)>1 -> multi
EOF

claims.behavior: The transcript writer and the project-directory encoder handle astral-plane characters by OPPOSITE conventions: the writer emits them verbatim as 4-byte UTF-8 and never as an escaped surrogate pair (over the whole live corpus - 66 top-level transcripts, 803,946 lines - 8,633 lines, 1.074%, carry a 4-byte UTF-8 lead byte in 0xF0-0xF4, and 0 lines carry a real `\udXXX` surrogate escape; exactly 1 line matches a naive surrogate regex, but its backslash run is EVEN, so those six characters are literal text quoted inside a tool result rather than an escape the writer produced), while the cwd encoder counts the same character as TWO UTF-16 code units and emits TWO dashes into the directory name.
claims.depends: csift must not carry either rule across: the verbatim-UTF-8 transcript convention is what keeps a non-ASCII (emoji, CJK) needle prefilter-eligible against raw line bytes - the needle-safety predicate escapes only `"`, C0 controls and DEL - while the same emoji sitting in a cwd must be re-encoded unit-wise by `path::encode_cwd` to two dashes or the project directory is not found. Applying the encoder's UTF-16 view to search needles, or the writer's codepoint view to the encoder, breaks one surface silently in each direction.
claims.instrument: Writer side: python over every `~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl` - count a line if any of its raw bytes is in 0xF0..=0xF4, and separately if a match of `\\u[dD][89abAB][0-9a-fA-F]{2}` is preceded by an ODD run of consecutive backslash bytes (the parity guard is required: without it the corpus returns 1 false positive, a doubled backslash in quoted content). Counting rule: one observation per whole line, not prefix-bounded. Whole-corpus rather than a random sample, so a stranger reruns the identical number. Measured 2026-09-02 at CC 2.1.258: 803,946 lines, 8,633 four-byte-lead lines, 0 real surrogate escapes. claims.behavior: Claude Code folds settings from a fixed FIVE-scope cascade, in order: userSettings, projectSettings, localSettings, flagSettings, policySettings (the source array at 157403765; the selector at 157430948 filters that array and always re-adds the last two, never reordering). The fold runs one accumulator over the scopes in that order with a merge whose customizer returns undefined for a plain scalar (157455238), so a scope read LATER overwrites a scalar such as plansDirectory set earlier - i.e. a --settings flag file and a managed policy file both override user, project and local. Each scope anchors its file differently (157435647): user under the config home, project and policy at the cwd, local at the canonical git root when there is one. The plans-directory resolver (159250888) reads the merged value, joins a relative value to the process's current project cwd through the same getter that stamps every record's top-level cwd (157582764: the async-local cwd, else the project cwd, the original cwd only when that getter throws), refuses a result that escapes that cwd (159251264), and falls back to join(config-home,'plans') (159250345). The resolved directory is memoized on first access, so the binding follows the cwd as it stood early in the session, before any tracked-shell cd moved the per-record value. Specimen (2026-09-03): all 21 plan_mode attachments in the corpus, across 18 transcripts, name the fallback directory; no scope on this host sets plansDirectory, so the configured branch has no on-disk specimen here.
claims.depends: csift's slug-only binding calls plans_dir(root) with root = the transcript's FIRST recorded cwd (src/plan/slug.rs first_cwd, the earliest instant csift can observe), reads user, project and local in that precedence from that root, joins and containment-checks against it, and falls back to <claude-home>/plans. Before v0.10.2 the root was the slug-carrying record's own cwd, which can already have drifted into a subdirectory: the plan file was then joined under the subdirectory and a project-scope plansDirectory was silently dropped. Two known divergences follow from the five-scope cascade: csift reads only the three FILE scopes, so a plansDirectory set in a --settings flag file or in managed policy settings - both of which override all three - is invisible to it; and csift anchors the local scope at the same root it uses for the project scope, whereas the harness anchors local at the canonical git root, so the two disagree when a session's root is not that git root. A session resumed from another directory re-memoizes in the harness, which the first-record instrument cannot see (documented limit).

claims.behavior: csift's `minted_at_compaction` flag means exactly what its code says - the first slug-carrying record is itself a `system`/`compact_boundary` - and it is only ever set on the `slug-only` fallback path. The boundary-first shape has a traced producer: both compaction drivers await the post-compact attachment build gNe (164833974 and 164839486 -> 164850720) BEFORE the boundary record is constructed, and gNe's plan probe p2o (164852199) reaches getPlanFilePath, so a session that has never had a slug gets one MINTED there at its first compaction (the mint itself, and the only place a value enters the map, is at 159247592); the record literal stamps slug:W from the memo of the session id (166105359), which is undefined and therefore omitted before the first mint, so the first carrier is simply the first record written after the first mint. A slug can also be minted during a turn at plan-mode entry (165738400), which is why other transcripts have an attachment, assistant or user record as their first carrier; which mint site ran first for any individual non-boundary-first transcript has not been attributed. Measured 2026-09-02 over the 26 slug-bearing top-level transcripts, the first slug carrier is one of FOUR record types: `assistant` 12, `attachment` 5, `system`/`compact_boundary` 5, `user` 4. Exactly 8 transcripts carry no `plan_mode` attachment at all and therefore bind `slug-only`; of those, 3 are boundary-first (`minted_at_compaction:true`), 1 is assistant-first and 4 are attachment-first (`minted_at_compaction:false`). Same date, two supporting specimens: a boundary-first slug-only transcript with 2,083 slug-bearing records and one distinct value, and an assistant-first transcript with 69,933 slug-bearing records and one distinct value.
claims.depends: csift sets `minted_at_compaction` when the first slug carrier is a compact boundary. It is a positive signal that a slug arrived at a compaction rather than at Plan-Mode entry, but it is NOT a two-way discriminator for whether Plan Mode ran - `binding_source` is what carries that, and a `slug-only` binding with `minted_at_compaction:false` is the common case (5 of 8 measured on 2026-09-02).

claims.behavior: The human-versus-automation discriminator lives on the DELIVERED twin, never on the queue line: the `queued_command` attachment carries `commandMode` in {`task-notification` 2,106, `prompt` 226}, and the delivered user record carries `origin.kind` in {`task-notification` 2,804, `human` 2,482, `peer` 57, `coordinator` 49} plus `promptSource` in {`system` 2,861, `typed` 2,564, `queued` 104}. `promptSource` alone is NOT a draft discriminator: measured drafts were 315 `typed` against 2 `queued` while finals were 317/317 `typed`.
claims.depends: csift does not model `origin` or `promptSource` today and classifies by content shape instead; these are the structural fields any future authorship or dispatch assertion would have to key on, and the draft census is why `promptSource` cannot stand in for the superseded-draft rule.

claims.behavior: Human prose enqueued into the input queue does not reliably become a user record: counting enqueue lines only, over 6 sessions (n=782 texts, whitespace-normalized), 72% match a later user record exactly and 81% match by prefix - so 19-28% of typed queue text never becomes a user record at all. An earlier ~61%-never figure counted every queue operation, remove lines included, over 3 sessions and is superseded by the narrower count.
claims.depends: the gap is why `user.queued` exists as its own searchable leaf: for that 19-28% the queue line is the only on-disk copy of what the operator typed, and a `-t user.message` search over it would report a definitive absence.
claims.instrument: For one session extract every `enqueue` line and test its `content` against `csift search -F <text> @<id> -t user.message`; counting rule = enqueue lines only (never remove or dequeue), one comparison per enqueued text, with exact-string and 40-char-prefix matches counted separately.

claims.behavior: A background task completion notification is delivered on THREE carriers: a `queue-operation` line with `operation:"enqueue"`, an `attachment` whose payload `type` is `queued_command` (carrying `commandMode:"task-notification"`), and - only when the session was idle - a `type:"user"` string record. 1,000 of 2,502 returned main-lane shells (40%) never produce a user record at all, so for those the queue line and the attachment are the only trace.
claims.depends: the csift background scanner reads all three carrier shapes; restricting it to `type:"user"` records would miss 40% of shell completions and leave them permanently `open`, inflating the idle-background-open verdict.
claims.instrument: Take a known background task id from a launch result and `rg -n '<its id>' <the main transcript>`, then classify each matching line by its `type` field; counting rule = one carrier observation per matching line, bucketed into `queue-operation` / `attachment` / `user`. A launch with a queue row but no user row is a mid-turn delivery.

Carrier-set distribution: 1,193 {queue-operation, user(string), +hook_success attachment}, 1,015 {queue-operation, attachment:queued_command}, 311 {queue-operation, user(string)}, 1 {queue-operation}. Returned shells with NO user-record carrier: 1,016 = 40%. The queue-operation carrier is present on all 2,520. The `queued_command` attachment appears on exactly the 1,015 launches that have no user record - i.e. mid-turn delivery. No <task-notification> element was found in any subagent transcript; the 9 subagent user-string records matching <tool-use-id> all begin `[SYSTEM NOTIFICATION - NOT USE...` and the 171 other subagent occurrences are inside tool_result payloads.
checks.rule: One launch observation per assistant tool_use block with run_in_background true in a non-subagent transcript; one carrier observation per (launch id, carrier kind) pair, joined on the exact <tool-use-id> string. 'returned' = at least one carrier; 'no user record' = no carrier of kind type:"user" with string content.
checks.note: The strongest result in this batch: the three-carrier model is not just observed, it partitions cleanly - a queue-operation on 100% of returned shells, a queued_command attachment on exactly the 1,015 with no user record, a user string record on the other 1,504. Restricting the scan to user records would indeed lose 40% of shell completions.

claims.behavior: Claude Code writes a `type:"system"` / `subtype:"turn_duration"` record per assistant turn, not per user record (4,580 such records against roughly 40,000 user records in the same corpus). Its payload is integers only - `durationMs` (median 134,688 ms) and `messageCount` (a running total) - and unlike the metadata cache lines it DOES carry `uuid`, `timestamp` and `parentUuid` with `isMeta:false`, plus `slug` on about 93% of records and `sessionKind` rarely.
claims.depends: csift promotes it to the gated leaf `harness.meta.turn-duration`, renders a FABRICATED `[turn duration: ...]` key=value excerpt from exactly these fields, and - because the record carries a uuid and a timestamp - lets `show --uuid` and `show --line` address it flag-free.

The recap text is pushed onto the same in-memory transcript array the REPL keeps (181822892), the array the human's own messages are appended to (180710536), so it really is a member of the conversation the query normalizes. The builder that turns that array into API messages then drops it: the first statement of the message-build loop skips any record for which LP holds (165959679), and LP holds for a progress record, for a virtual or api-error placeholder, and for a `type:"system"` record whose subtype is not `local_command` (165953664); the single surviving system subtype is checked by UWt (165947398) and survives only by being re-minted as a user message. The request body maps only the survivors' `message.role` and `message.content` (165407936), so a recap can never appear in a request and a record with no `message{}` could not be mapped at all. The recap itself is produced by a separate one-turn sub-query with querySource away_summary, tools denied and skipTranscript true (168868261), whose own messages are never persisted; the timer is armed only when the awaySummaryEnabled setting is on (181824717) and fires only while the terminal is blurred (181823457), behind a skip chain (181821805) that bails on a stale cache, a rate limit, a draft input, pending background work or a pending wakeup. This corpus holds 11 of the 18. Census 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one observation per parsed record whose top-level type is "system": 13,051 records - stop_hook_summary 5,785, turn_duration 4,775, away_summary 1,682, scheduled_task_fire 459, compact_boundary 235, model_refusal_fallback 51, api_error 29, local_command 15, agents_killed 10, informational 8, model_refusal_no_fallback 2. The other seven (permission_retry, bridge_status, cloud_session_status, memory_saved, file_snapshot, model_fallback, model_consent_fallback) have zero specimens here, which is a corpus fact and not evidence they cannot be written. Shapes, one observation per parsed record: all 459 scheduled_task_fire records carry a content string opening 'Claude resuming /loop wakeup (' - the loop arm's template (187387332), never the plain 'Running scheduled task' arm - and a fire sits beside the delivered wakeup, an isMeta:true user record within 2s in 97.4 percent of cases at the 2026-09-02 check, plus a queue-operation enqueue line. claims.behavior: An assistant record's `message.usage` object comes in exactly two shapes, and which one a record carries is decided by WHEN the record was flushed, not by the build. The binary declares one usage schema (163860106) naming eleven keys - input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens (nullable), cache_read_input_tokens (nullable), server_tool_use (nullable), service_tier (nullable), cache_creation (nullable), inference_geo (nullable, optional), speed (nullable, optional), iterations (optional), output_tokens_details (nullable, optional) - and seeds a zero-value template with the same eleven (160103067). A per-block record is built at content_block_stop as {message:{...<the message_start message>,content:...}} (165442985), so it carries the RAW API usage and a null stop_reason; the eleven-key object is only assembled later by the message-level merge (165472361) and stamped onto every accumulated record by the message_delta fan-out (165444727), so a record already yielded from the earlier flush keeps the raw shape permanently. Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one observation per parsed assistant record whose message.usage is an object, restricted to the three neighbouring builds 2.1.257/258/259 (40,487 records): there are exactly TWO key sets - a 7-key raw shape (cache_creation, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, inference_geo, input_tokens, output_tokens, service_tier) on 32,127 records, every one of them with stop_reason null, and the 11-key schema shape on 8,360 records, every one with a real stop_reason. Version floor, same day, one observation per line whose bytes carry an assistant record type and a usage key, bucketed by the record's own version string (463,432 lines in 40 version buckets): no record written at or below 2.1.227 carries output_tokens_details - 0 of 352,798 across 28 buckets - and the literal enters the executable at 2.1.228 (absent at 2.1.227, present at 2.1.228; the two are adjacent in the version list). The converse is false: above the floor only 47,911 of 110,634 records (43.3 percent) carry the key, every bucket larger than 400 records is mixed (2.1.258: 3,242 of 12,897; 2.1.259: 4,338 of 26,245), and both shapes coexist inside single transcripts. Value shapes: the four token counts are integers, service_tier / speed / inference_geo strings, cache_creation / server_tool_use / output_tokens_details objects, and iterations an ARRAY of per-API-call usage objects.
claims.depends: csift's `TokenUsage` probe deserializes exactly four of the eleven keys (`input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`), and all four are present in BOTH shapes, so `csift stats` is untouched by the split; it reports no thinking-token split, no server-tool counts, no service tier and no inference geography. Any surface that ever reads `usage.output_tokens_details` must treat absence as NORMAL on a record with a null stop_reason at every build from 2.1.228 on - never as an old-build signal - because the missing key marks a per-block flush, not an old writer.
claims.instrument: Two instruments. (1) `strings -n 6` over the 2.1.258 binary for the literal usage schema and the literal zero-value usage template - both name exactly eleven keys. (2) Python over the transcript corpus: count each usage key across assistant records, once per record, reported separately for the version-current subset (records whose `version` is 2.1.258) and for a mixed-version sample.

claims.behavior: Every record carries a top-level version stamp naming the build that wrote it and a gitBranch field, and both can change inside one transcript - by different mechanisms. The version stamp is a constant of the WRITING PROCESS: the per-append stamper writes version:Uts (166074085) and Uts is fixed at build time (166065151), so an in-place upgrade changes nothing for a running process and a second stamp can appear only when a NEW process adopts the same file. That happens on a NON-FORK resume: the resume handler (181936945) reaches an adoption statement guarded on the fork flag (181939450) which points the writer at the existing transcript and re-appends the session metadata (166123513, and its storage twin at 166123786); a forked resume mints a new file instead. gitBranch is read once per append (166104693) from a cache-backed getter (157762344) whose watched git state invalidates on HEAD and on refs/heads/<branch> (157784128), so it changes on any append after a checkout. Both mechanisms are version-stable across the whole range this corpus spans: the adopt path is present and byte-equivalent in every build probed from 2.1.150 to 2.1.259, so no era caveat is needed. Corpus measurement 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root (7,968 files, workflow journals and the elicitation sidecar excluded): 7,967 of 7,968 carry a version stamp; 42 distinct build stamps span 2.1.150 to 2.1.259 - one build newer than the audited binary; 12 files carry more than one stamp; 29 adjacent transitions occur in physical line order and all 29 are upgrades, none a downgrade; the deepest single transcript carries 7 distinct stamps (2.1.150, 2.1.154, 2.1.156, 2.1.159, 2.1.177, 2.1.186, 2.1.191).

import json, collections
FIELDS = ['input_tokens', 'output_tokens', 'cache_read_input_tokens', 'cache_creation_input_tokens']
for f in [<three transcripts>]:
    per = collections.Counter(); byid = {}
    for line in open(f, errors='replace'):
        if '"usage"' not in line: continue
        try: r = json.loads(line)
        except Exception: continue
        m = r.get('message')
        if not isinstance(m, dict): continue
        u = m.get('usage')
        if not isinstance(u, dict): continue
        mdl = m.get('model') or '(unknown)'; mid = m.get('id')
        for fld in FIELDS:
            v = u.get(fld) or 0
            per[(mdl, fld)] += v
            k = (mdl, mid, fld)
            byid[k] = v if mid is None else max(byid.get(k, 0), v)
    ded = collections.Counter()
    for (mdl, mid, fld), v in byid.items(): ded[(mdl, fld)] += v
    for k in per: print(f, k, per[k], ded[k], per[k]/ded[k])

claims.behavior: A cloned transcript's copied records are REWRITTEN, not byte-copied: each carries the CLONING build's `version`, not the version the origin stamped on that same record. `uuid` and `timestamp` survive byte-identically, while `version`, `sessionId` and `sessionKind` are rewritten and `slug` is stripped. Measured on the one clone/origin pair in the corpus: all 558 shared uuids read 2.1.251 in the origin and 2.1.252 in the clone (0/558 equal), with identical timestamps, `slug` present->absent and `sessionKind` null->"bg".
claims.depends: csift reports `version_first` from the head window and `version` from the tail window, so a clone reports the clone-time build as its first - one of the visible symptoms of the fork.
claims.instrument: `csift search '' @<id> --count-by version` on the clone beside the same census on its origin is only SUGGESTIVE - the clone's single head version could in principle be the origin's own tail version. The decisive instrument is a uuid JOIN across the two transcripts: intersect the top-level `uuid` sets and compare `version` (and every other top-level field) on the shared records. Counting rule = one per shared uuid; the claim holds iff origin.version != clone.version on all of them.

claims.behavior: MECHANISM. The Read tool imposes no default line window: the handler defaults offset to 1 and limit to undefined (164904193), and the shipped prompt's 'reads up to 2000 lines' sentence (160024011, the constant at 160022498) instructs the model rather than the code. The numLines/totalLines pair an echo carries has TWO producing readers, forked on isFile() && size < 10485760 (161427310): the in-memory reader (161427688) and the streaming reader (161428784 / 161430555). Equality - a FULL read - is produced by three branches, not one: the in-memory early return when offset is 0, limit undefined and neither byte budget is set (161427777); the in-memory windowed loop whenever the window happens to cover every line (161428111); and the streaming end handler's resolve on an unwindowed pass (161431048), so a full-file verdict must be stated per reader, never binary-wide. On the Read tool's own path a partial has exactly TWO causes: a caller window (an offset and/or limit narrowing the kept range - the in-memory loop's bound and the streaming reader's identical per-chunk window test at 161429390), and the token-cap re-slice (164912181), the only cause that sets truncatedByTokenCap and itself gated to an unwindowed read (164911906). The streaming reader adds no third cause: its byte-truncation arm is unreachable from Read because that call never passes truncateOnByteLimit, so an unwindowed read of a file at or above the 10,485,760-byte fork ERRORS - the stream is destroyed with the size error - instead of echoing, while a windowed read of such a file, and any read of a non-regular target, does stream and echoes normally. The measured bytes come from one literal (164914065): numLines is the kept-line count, totalLines the reader's count, and truncatedByTokenCap is spread only when the cap arm ran. PROPORTION - a usage regularity no branch of the binary produces. Measured 2026-09-04 over every transcript under the projects root, one observation per toolUseResult.file echo carrying both integer counts: 8,719 echoes, 4,888 partial (56.1 percent), 3,831 full, 0 with numLines > totalLines. 179 of the partials carry truncatedByTokenCap (3.66 percent) and 1 FULL echo carries it, the single-line clip shape. The 2026-09-04 join of each partial back to its Read tool_use input attributed 4,709 to an explicit offset and/or limit, 178 to the cap alone and 1 to both, with 0 unattributed. The corpus cannot say which reader served a given partial - the echo records a window, not a file size - but no FULL echo came from the streaming reader, the largest full echo measured being far below the fork threshold.
claims.depends: csift's replay therefore spends most of its time on `PartialRead` splices rather than full anchors, which is why the gap accounting (`??? lines A..B unknown`) and not the anchor path is `recover`'s dominant correctness surface. The two causes are distinguishable on disk - truncatedByTokenCap names the cap, and its absence on a partial means a caller window - so recover never has to guess which one clipped a read; and because equality can come from a windowed read as well as from a full-file branch, csift must read numLines == totalLines as 'this window covered the file', not as 'the caller asked for the whole file'.

User input submitted while a turn is running never becomes a user record: the turn guard's tryStart returns null (181623439) and that arm re-enqueues every user message of the batch and returns before the batch's single append (181624300); the batch is buffered and never flushed once handed off (181586905); the queued input is drained back only while the guard is idle (181701890); and an item absorbed DURING the query is delivered as a queued_command attachment and consumed (164752640) rather than minted as a user record. Results drain back into the generator that issued the call (164583277), and the only join key written is the call id echoed on the result carrier (164578780). Corpus census 2026-09-03 over 7899 transcripts: 225906 joins resolved within one file - main 59757, subagent 35960, workflow 130189 - with 0 joins having a turn-opener candidate between call and result and 0 orphan results in every lane, 32 unreturned calls, and 14771 turn-opener candidates across 7846 of the 7899 files, so the test is not vacuous. claims.depends: Every Lnnnn header, every `csift show @<id> --line N` refetch pointer, the `show` and `verbatim` continuation pointers and `recover --file-lines` treat a physical line number as a durable address, and the ordinary append path supports that; the no-split property is also what lets the mmap reader capture the length at open and skip a torn trailing fragment (src/parse/lines.rs:18-21). The caveat rides with them: a tombstone removal, a local-GC compact rewrite or a remote hydration replace invalidates every line address at or below its cut, so a previously printed Lnnnn can go stale and - worse than a loud miss - silently address a different record. Only the removal path is ungated and reachable from an ordinary interactive lane; the compact rewrite needs an sdk-url resume with local GC armed and a file above 5 MiB, and the hydration replace needs a remote ingress or CCR v2 resume. A compaction in the ordinary sense leaves the addresses valid, because it appends.

claims.behavior: This claim's fact is csift's own, not Claude Code's: no code in the shipped 2.1.258 binary can produce it. An explicit `show` address that resolves to no record is a HARD failure, not an empty result - csift bails with `no such record(s): ` naming each miss and exits non-zero. A single `--line` token with no `..` is an explicit address; a `..` token is a clamping range that must still yield at least one record. Verified 2026-09-04 with csift 0.10.3: `show @<id> --line 999999 --raw` exits 1 with `csift: error: no such record(s): L999999 (file has N lines)`; the DEFAULT rendered path bails from a different site and exits 1 with a longer tail that names what an explicit address renders (message lines, attachment lines and the promoted non-record lines) instead of the line count; `--line 999998..999999 --raw` exits 1 the same way with the range spelled `L999998-999999`; and a valid `--line 1..2 --raw` exits 0 with two lines. The counting rule is exit code non-zero plus the literal `no such record(s): `; the suffix is path-dependent and must not be keyed on. The Claude Code half of this story - the transcript writer's append, remove, compact and hydrate behavior - is a separate proposition and belongs in its own claim.
claims.depends: The premise this enforcement rests on is that a physical line number is a durable address, and that premise is CONDITIONAL, not absolute. It holds on the ordinary append path, which only ever appends whole lines. Three located paths renumber a live transcript: `performRemoveByUuid` (166095622), UNGATED, which truncates at the removed record and writes the tail back, or falls back to filtering and rewriting the whole file at or below 52428800 bytes, and which an ordinary interactive lane reaches through the REPL refusal-continuation branch (181619551, wrapper 166122929) and the stream tombstone handler (181621337, wrapper 166122853); `performCompactTranscript` (166098791), which renames a filtered temp over the original and is gated on `store.localGcEnabled` (class default false at 166076591, armed only from the sdkUrl resume branch at 179355990) plus the 5242880-byte floor at 166067515; and the remote hydration REPLACE, `KQ` (157607804) opening the file in `w` mode, from the v1 session-ingress hydrator at 166132033 and the CCR v2 resume hydrator at 166139023 - the last of these is NOT size-gated. After any of the three, csift's hard failure bounds only ONE failure mode, an address past EOF; it cannot detect the other, an address that still resolves and now names a DIFFERENT record. So the guarantee is: a stale refetch never comes back as a silent empty, and it never comes back as wrong content unless one of those three paths has run on that file.

claims.behavior: Claude Code serializes every transcript record with JSON.stringify and no replacer (the writer j5 at 156850249, `function j5(e){return JSON.stringify(e)+"\n"}`, selected for every queued entry by the drain at 166086450) and appends the resulting string with no encoding option, so non-ASCII text reaches disk as verbatim UTF-8 rather than as a \uXXXX escape. The ONE escape a well-formed JSON.stringify still emits for a codepoint >= U+0080 is a LONE (unpaired) surrogate, and the corpus does exhibit it. Census of the whole projects root on 2026-09-04, one observation per non-blank line bounded at the first 4,000 bytes, an escape counted only when the backslash run before the u is odd: 8,157 jsonl transcripts, 1,393,149 non-blank lines, 374,147 lines (26.86%) carrying a byte >= 0x80, 11,897 escape-regex hits of which exactly 1 is writer-emitted - a `\ud83c` left where a <persisted-output> preview was truncated mid-emoji - and the other 11,896 a literal two-character backslash-u inside quoted content. Restricted to the 68 top-level transcripts (812,882 non-blank lines) the same rule gives 181,069 non-ASCII lines (22.27%) and 0 writer-emitted escapes, reproducing the 2026-09-02 check's 67-file figures (804,007 lines, 178,918 non-ASCII, 22.25%, 0 escapes).
claims.depends: This is why csift's needle-safety predicate (json_escapes_in_string, src/search/matcher.rs) keeps non-ASCII needles prefilter-eligible, and why the product can promise regex over CJK at all: if the writer switched to ASCII-safe output, every multi-byte pattern would stop matching at the byte prefilter, before any counter could see it - the silent-drop failure `required_needles` exists to prevent. The lone-surrogate exception does not reopen that hole and is not silent. A Rust pattern cannot contain an unpaired surrogate, so no expressible needle can be lost to it; and when such a line lands, serde_json refuses the escape, so csift books the line rather than dropping it quietly - measured on 2026-09-04 with csift 0.10.3 against the single corpus specimen, `search` reports skipped_lines 1, `stats` prints "1 malformed line(s) skipped", a rendered `show --line` address bails with "no such record(s)", and `show --line N --raw` still returns the bytes.

claims.behavior: The usage object persisted on an assistant record is not the API's object but the running result of a per-delta merge: the stream loop folds each message_delta through FY (call at 165443569) and FY (165471565) rebuilds `cache_creation_input_tokens` as the API's flat value when it is non-null and greater than zero, otherwise the nested sum o = (ephemeral_1h ?? 0) + (ephemeral_5m ?? 0), otherwise the accumulator's own flat value (the branch at 165472012) - while the nested `cache_creation` object falls back to {...accumulator.cache_creation} when o is 0, a DIFFERENT fallback source. The completed accumulator is then stamped on every per-block record of the message (165444727). The nested pair therefore very nearly PARTITIONS the flat field without being guaranteed to. Census of the whole projects root on 2026-09-04, one observation per record whose message.usage.cache_creation is an object, missing sub-keys read as 0, exact integer equality: 464,002 records carry it, 463,865 agree (99.970%) and 137 disagree (0.030%). Every disagreement is one-hour-cache-specific: all 137 have a zero 5m bucket and a non-zero 1h bucket, 101 of them with a flat field of 0 (the whole 1h amount missing from the flat field) and 36 with a non-zero flat field that still differs. All 137 sit in top-level transcripts, where the same rule gives 135,592 records and 99.899% agreement - the scope the 2026-09-02 check's 133,935 / 99.898% figures actually described.

It is a different axis from the per-agent lifecycle status csift computes from a transcript tail. The journal does NOT carry a run status - a journal line's only discriminator is `type`, whose observed values are `started`, `result` and `failed`.
claims.depends: csift reads the value with a plain string field read and prints it unchanged on `kind:"run"` rows; tightening it into a closed set would drop or mislabel a run state the runtime later adds.

The binary carries its own validator for that pair of shapes at 156729976: Sn = new RegExp('^a(?:' + Xe + '-)?[0-9a-f]{16}$') with Xe = "[\\w-]{1,63}". The name-embedded form is not teammate-exclusive: the in-process teammate spawner mints c = o.resumableAgentId ?? Oh(name) (176267563), and the fork launcher on its kind:"fork" path mints n = Oh(e.agentLifecycle.allocateName(...)) (172858492). Either way the minted string becomes the lane id in the agent runner (Cn = B?.agentId ? B.agentId : Oh() at 163774605), rides every record of that lane (163784699), and appendEntry's dedup-transcript arm routes a sidechain record carrying an agentId to Ud(uo(agentId)) (166107661), which is agent-<id>.jsonl (159262698) - so the canonical id is exactly the file basename. Corpus on 2026-09-04, one observation per lane file: 7,831 subagent transcripts, all 7,831 matching the binary's own validator; 7,666 carry the nameless a + 16 hex form (17 characters, every one leading with a) and 165 are name-embedded. Of those 165, 164 have a sibling meta with taskKind:"in_process_teammate" (164/164 matching ^a[\w-]{1,63}-[0-9a-f]{16}$, 135/164 with a dash inside the name half, 164/164 carrying no toolUseId) and 1 has no taskKind at all - a fork lane whose meta reads agentType "fork" with isFork true.

Because the shape is not teammate-exclusive, is_teammate_agent_id also accepts a fork lane id - correct for routing, and wrong only as a name: the teammate discriminator is the sibling meta's taskKind:"in_process_teammate", which is what make_subagent already upgrades on, never the id shape.

claims.behavior: A subagent's returned message reaches its parent by one of three carriers, not one: the synchronous tool_result text (the Agent tool's completed return at 163931233, whose payload holds the child's final assistant content), the child transcript's tail assistant text when the parent result was the async launch ack (163925044), or the workflow journal's `result` event payload - the agent() hook's closure $t at 172615720 appends {type:"result",key,agentId,result} only when a journal and a key exist and the result is not null. A node that resolves through none of the three carries a null source and no returned message, and that population has a producer: when a workflow agent's result IS null, $t routes to the failed closure $e (172615399), which appends {type:"failed"} carrying no result payload - and returns having appended nothing at all when the run's abort signal is already set - so the journal keeps a `started` event with no `result`. Measured on 2026-09-04 with csift 0.10.3 over 27 sessions and 8,084 subagent nodes, one node per subagent transcript and exactly one source per node: workflow-journal 6,548, async-child-tail 482, sync-tool-result 364, null 690. Of the 690 null-source nodes, 689 are workflow lanes and 1 is a teammate lane. Independently, the 166 workflow journals in the corpus carry 7,061 `started`, 6,372 `result` and 61 `failed` events, and exactly 689 started agent ids have no result event - 61 of them with an explicit failed event and 628 with neither.
claims.depends: csift implements all three paths and records which one answered as `returned_message_source` (src/agents/json.rs, src/agents/render.rs); dropping the async-child-tail fallback loses the report for every background-launched agent, and dropping the journal path loses it for the dominant workflow kind. A null source is not a csift miss: for a workflow lane it means the journal holds no result event for that agent, so there is nothing on disk to read - which is why the null share tracks the journals' result-less started keys one for one.

claims.behavior: The lane a completion notification is delivered to is chosen per notification; it is not fixed to the main transcript. The agent-completion enqueuer (164953374) resolves the destination first with eVe({ownerAgentId, keepaliveReason, delivering, taskRegistry}), and eVe (164954861) is a liveness decision whose last statement is `return _&&e?uo(e):Ze()` (164955053): the owner agent's OWN lane while that owner is live or its status is "running", and Ze() otherwise; the enqueued item carries that lane as agentId (164954442). The background-shell completion handler Ddt (164968006) is not liveness-gated at all - its inline enqueue addresses `agentId: v ?? Ze()` (164968716), the owning agent's lane whenever a subagent started the shell. Ze() itself (156787676) is the CURRENT lane, not a main-lane constant: it returns uo(sessionId) whenever there is an agent context and falls back to the main agent id only otherwise. Across all 56 mode:"task-notification" enqueue sites, 49 pass, default to or omit agentId:Ze() and 7 name an owner lane explicitly - one of them (163710736) with no liveness test whatever - and no site pins the destination to the main transcript. On the drain side t9e (162030912) folds per lane: the main thread takes items satisfying fg (agentId === Ze(), 160411638), a child lane takes items whose mode is task-notification and whose agentId equals its own; appendEntry then writes a sidechain record carrying an agentId to Ud(uo(agentId)) (166107661, 159262698). A child delivery is also FRAMED differently from a main one: the resume driver mints it as xe({content: dpe(d, c), origin: c, isMeta: true}) (175692385) and dpe's task-notification case (166046409) prefixes the [SYSTEM NOTIFICATION - NOT USER INPUT] block through sbt (160018067), so the tag does not sit at content start. Census on 2026-09-04, one observation per type:"user" record whose OWN message text contains the tag: 88 main transcripts hold 2,949 such records, 2,887 with the tag at content start and the same 2,887 carrying origin.kind "task-notification"; 7,908 subagent lanes hold 79, of which 0 start with the tag and 9 carry origin.kind "task-notification" - spread over 4 lane files, every one isMeta true and isSidechain true with the tag at index 494 behind the preamble, 8 written by build 2.1.252 and 1 by the audited 2.1.258. Main-lane delivery is therefore the dominant OUTCOME of a corpus whose task owners had settled, not a routing invariant.

claims.behavior: A turn opens on any of FOUR record shapes, not just genuine human prose, and each shape has its own path in the 2.1.258 binary. (1) GENUINE USER: the prompt-queue drain classifies each submission's source and hands it to the prompt handler (181584452); the record builder's content-shape branch writes either a text-block array when attachments ride along or the raw value as a STRING (169779554 for the array arm, 169779835 for the string arm) - the two shapes csift's genuine-user test accepts. (2) ANSWERED AskUserQuestion: the dialog submit returns behavior allow with the answers map and the annotations (181436561); the tool's call() emits {questions, answers (defaulting to {}), response?, annotations?, afkTimeoutMs?} (164277926); and the carrier write puts the model-facing tool_result block and that structured object onto one role user record in a single statement (162940162), so the answer arrives as a non-errored tool_result carrier. (3) TOOL-USE REJECTION WITH A TYPED INSTRUCTION: the REPL rejection handler calls cancelAndAbort with the typed feedback (176224707), whose ternary selects the template ending in the delimiter only when the typed message is non-blank (176196480) - a bare rejection takes the other arm and is not a boundary - and the denial carrier is written with is_error true and a STRING toolUseResult (164447097). (4) INBOUND PEER MESSAGE, with two traced deliveries: the inbox poller, constructed and started for the session lifetime (181722910), drains only when it is enabled, the session is not loading and no dialog is up (181720143), formats the WHOLE pending batch in one call and submits it (181720688), and the submit builds a bare user record and runs it (181636577); and the in-process teammate runner, whose new_messages handler formats the drained array (176257992) into a record (176258983) that is handed to the agent runner as promptMessages (176260570) and reaches the lane file through the runner's seed append (163784699). All four end at the same append, which stamps the envelope and a promptId onto EVERY user record (166105477) - so promptId presence identifies no particular writer. A third peer-delivery family is only partly traced: on 2026-09-04, 47 of the 909 peer-tag string-content user records under the projects root are isMeta with an origin of kind "peer" and carry <agent-message> sections (26 with the key set from/kind/senderTaskId, 21 with body/from/kind/name/senderTaskId); the SendMessage in-process delivery mints exactly that origin and delivers it with isMeta true (175782487), and the preamble is applied at record-mint time by the origin-driven applier the prompt builder calls (166048114), but the hop from that delivery to the record mint is not read. claims.behavior: isMeta:true on a type:"user" record is an AUTHORSHIP flag stamped by the injecting call site, not derived from the content: the one user-record factory takes isMeta as a named parameter and copies it straight onto the record (165936023). Two injectors are read end to end in 2.1.258. The resume path's interrupted_turn branch injects a continuation prompt (163207700) whose text comes from a helper returning the CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_PROMPT environment value or, failing that, the fixed sentence "Continue from where you left off." (163204432) - which is why the sentence is a PREFIX and not always the whole content: the background revival respawn sets a longer restarted variant (167486480) and the runner spawn sets a moved-to-a-new-runner variant (166506250). The local-command caveat injector writes its own isMeta:true pseudo-turn (165936931). Measured on 2026-09-04 over 68 uuid-named top-level transcripts: 1,426 isMeta:true type user records (690 with string content, 736 with block-array content), led by an "[Image: source: ...]" marker 661, a <local-command-caveat> wrapper 165, a skill base-directory preamble 43, a "Stop hook feedback: ..." line 30, and the continuation sentence 7 - all 7 the bare form, neither longer variant occurring in this corpus. The image, skill-preamble and stop-hook buckets have no injector traced here; only the continuation and caveat buckets do.
claims.depends: csift gates isMeta out of is_genuine_user before any content inspection (src/model/predicates.rs), so a meta pseudo-turn never opens a turn and never enters the user.message census - verified by the claim's 2026-09-02 check with the strongest available instrument, a raw sweep of every user.message record in the top-level corpus finding no isMeta among them. Recognized markers reparent to harness.schedule.* / harness.meta.*; the continuation test is trim_start().starts_with(...) (src/model/markers.rs), which is what makes it survive the two longer 2.1.258 variants. An isMeta record matching no known marker classifies EMPTY - not merely unlabeled but invisible to a scan (40 of 41 skill-preamble records returned no hit at all on 2026-09-02) - so a novel hook wrapper can never be mistaken for the operator.
claims.instrument: `rg -c '"isMeta":true' <transcript>` against `csift search '' @<id> --count-by label` (no `user.message` key may cover them), and `rg -c 'Continue from where you left off\.' ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl` against `csift search 'Continue from where you left off' -t harness.schedule.continuation -c`. Counting rule: one per raw line for rg, one per classified record for csift.

claims.behavior: A subagent transcript's FIRST record is an isSidechain:true type:"user" seed carrying the spawn prompt. The Agent tool's call handler (163908866) takes the non-fork arm of the seed-builder branch (163919675) and mints exactly one string-content user record; the chain is handed to insertMessageChain with isSidechain hardcoded true (166114240), the envelope literal stamps isSidechain and agentId onto every record (166105359), and appendEntry's dedup-transcript arm routes such a record to the per-agent file (166107780) - so a sidechain seed can never land in a top-level transcript. A FORK child instead leads with a type:"fork-context-ref" line carrying exactly agentId, parentSessionId, parentLastUuid and contextLength, written on the runner's fork branch (163784470); but its directive seed does NOT follow immediately. ONE flag in the Agent tool - the subagent_type resolves to the fork type (constant at 159196188) AND that type is available (163910331) - selects BOTH the fork seed builder and the forkContextMessages argument (163921718) that alone can satisfy the fork-head branch's identity test, and the builder (163882619, returning at 163883130) returns TWO records: a re-minted copy of the parent's last assistant message (new uuid, content array copied) and a user record holding one tool_result per copied tool_use carrying the template that opens "Fork started" plus the fork directive text; only the degenerate no-tool_use arm returns a single record, and even that is a text-BLOCK array. So the record after a fork head is an ASSISTANT record and the child's directive seed is the THIRD record. The runner concatenates the inherited context ahead of the child's own messages (163774706), so the fork branch's slice drops the inherited PREFIX and keeps the child's own records; the assistant-first ordering comes from the seed builder, not from the slice. That coupling is NOT recent: the identical two-record builder and the identical one-flag coupling are present in every cached build read - 2.1.191, 2.1.215, 2.1.216, 2.1.219, 2.1.221, 2.1.222, 2.1.224, 2.1.228, 2.1.232, 2.1.233, 2.1.251 and 2.1.258 - so the fork head and the two-record seed cannot be separated through the Agent tool's fork arm in any of them, and the single contrary corpus lane has no identified producer. Corpus on 2026-09-04, one observation per lane file over records 1-3: 7,908 subagent lanes, 7,875 opening with the sidechain user seed (all with STRING content) and 33 with a fork-context-ref head whose key set is exactly the four fields above; record 2 after a fork head is assistant / isSidechain true with block content 32 times (18 stamped 2.1.233, 14 stamped 2.1.251) and a plain string-content user seed once (stamped 2.1.220, its lane meta naming the fork agent type), and record 3 is a user record carrying text plus tool_result 32 of 32, every one holding the Fork started template. 0 of the 68 uuid-named top-level transcripts carry any isSidechain:true line.
claims.depends: csift deliberately does NOT gate isSidechain out of is_genuine_user (src/model/predicates.rs), so list's per-subagent preview can treat the seed as the subagent's first user message - gating it would silently blank every subagent preview for zero real benefit - and the seed classifies agent.communication.inbox with a parent-to-self direction while the per-surface scan owns the subagent-versus-parent context. That holds for the 7,875 ordinary lanes and fails on the 33 fork lanes: there the first user record is the THIRD one, and because it carries tool_result blocks beside its text it is not a genuine user record at all. Measured with csift 0.10.3 on 2026-09-04, 32 of the 33 fork lanes report first_user null (the exception is the single string-seed lane), and reading one back shows the fork head as a non-record line, the assistant copy as agent.communication.sent and the directive seed as agent.communication.inbox rendered from the Fork started template rather than from the directive text.

claims.behavior: When the user recalls a sent message with escape, edits it and re-sends, Claude Code leaves the ORIGINAL on disk: the draft and the delivered resend are separate `type:"user"` records sharing ONE non-null `parentUuid`, and only the last in file order was delivered. The shared parent is usually a turn-end anchor record - measured parents were a `stop_hook_summary` system record 133 times, `turn_duration` 83, `away_summary` 80, an interrupt marker 19 and an assistant record once.
claims.depends: `superseded_draft_indices` keeps the LAST opener per `parentUuid` and marks the earlier siblings superseded, and `group_turn_indices_deduped` drops them entirely from turn numbering, so an edited-away message can never resurface as a phantom turn or leak its abandoned text into a neighbour. The signal is parent-uuid IDENTITY, not text similarity, which would miss the common prepend/insert edit; distinct real turns never share a parentUuid, and a record with a null/empty parent is never grouped.
claims.instrument: Group all turn-opening user records of one transcript by `parentUuid` and count groups of size greater than one (counting rule: drafts = group size minus one, one per group), then cross-validate against csift's own `N superseded draft(s)` footer. Measured draft rates over four sessions: 11% (62 genuine / 7 drafts), 26% (1,216 / 317), 6% (86 / 5), 3% (32 / 1).

claims.behavior: Two neighbouring shapes leave no user record, and they differ in evidential standing. (a) THE QUEUE HALF is fully written. A queued text edited before dispatch never becomes a type:"user" record: the REPL submit dispatcher enqueues every typed prompt and returns early while a turn is running (181580347); the admission gate pushes the item and logs it only when the item is not marked unlogged and only when its value is a string (162035115); the writer builds {type:"queue-operation", operation, timestamp, sessionId, content?, reason?} (162031901) and hands it to the default sink, which ends in insertQueueOperation and appendEntry with queue-operation routed "always" (162029731). The two escapes are the drain that logs each item and returns the joined text to the INPUT BOX without constructing any message record (162041220), and the mid-turn fold, which emits the item as a queued_command attachment and consumes it with reason "absorbed_mid_turn" (164752627). So the typed text survives only in the queue-operation lines. Corpus on 2026-09-04: 39 transcripts carry parsed type:"queue-operation" lines - enqueue 6,924 (all with content), popAll 109 (all with content), dequeue 3,534 (none), remove 3,273 of which 2,477 carry content. Of the enqueues, 949 are human prose (content not opening with "<"); whitespace-normalized, 610 of those match a later user record in the same file exactly (64.3 percent), 126 more match by their first 200 characters (13.3 percent, 77.6 percent combined) and 213 never match (22.4 percent). (b) THE ESC-RECALL HALF is a negative closed by enumeration, not a written path. The local recall entry rewinds and then puts the recalled text back into the input box (180778537); the rewind itself slices the in-memory snapshot and replaces it with no append anywhere (180776684), and the transcript file is append-only, so the recalled message's own record stays exactly as written and nothing new is written. At 2.1.258 a rewind CAN leave one positive artifact - a last-prompt line carrying leafUuid and rewound:true (166113611) - but it names the rewind event and the surviving leaf, never the recalled text, and of the six occurrences of that function name exactly one is the definition, four are call sites and one is an unrelated same-named component; only the remote/bridge rewind handler passes the flag, building {rewound:true} and handing it to both the internal-event mirror and the transcript append (179289648). In this corpus that marker has zero specimens: 0 lines carry it against 29,662 last-prompt lines on 2026-09-04. So the recalled text is never re-written, and no rewind marker exists here at all.
claims.depends: csift's user.unsent covers only SUPERSEDED drafts - the esc-recall and edit-resend pairs detected by a shared parentUuid (src/model/grouping.rs) - never "every unsent message". The queue-only class is a separate and larger set, reachable solely under the gated user.queued leaf, and csift documents the join rule and its counting basis instead of asserting a bare dispatched flag: the queue-operation line carries no join key, and roughly a fifth to a quarter of enqueued human prose never becomes a user record. A message recalled and then abandoned has no sibling and stays undetectable from the local path, which writes nothing; the version-scoped caveat is that a rewind driven through the remote/bridge handler can write a rewound:true last-prompt line, so if such a line ever appears in a corpus csift reads, that half has to be re-decided rather than re-asserted - the line names the surviving leaf, which would give csift a second instrument for abandoned branches.
claims.instrument: Extract every `queue-operation` enqueue `content` and test whether the whitespace-normalized text appears as a later `type:"user"` record's string content or `text` block - `csift search '' @<id> -t user.queued --format json` against `-t user.message`. Counting rule: enqueue lines only, human prose only, one comparison per enqueued text; 'exact' = full-string equality, 'prefix' = the first 200 characters as a substring. An earlier figure of about 61% never-dispatched (54 of 88 texts, three-session sample) was measured over ALL queue operations and is superseded by the human-prose-only figures.

claims.behavior: A Windows session's projects-directory basename is letter-led rather than dash-led: the sanitizer applies no slash, case or colon pre-normalization, so the cwd `C:\Users\x` encodes to `C--Users-x` (the drive letter passes through; `:` and `\` each become exactly one dash) and a UNC root `\\server\share` encodes to `--server-share`.
claims.depends: csift's `@`-token grammar has to recognize both shapes: `is_drive_encoded_token` accepts `<letter>--...` as an encoded project dir (bare or `@`-prefixed) while the UNC form is reachable only as `@--server-...`, because a bare `--`-leading token is reserved for the mistyped-flag guard; a drive-shaped token that matches no directory falls through to real-path resolution, since it can also be a genuine relative path. Without those arms a Windows project directory is unreachable by any target form.
claims.instrument: Only a Claude Code session started on Windows produces the directory: run one and list `~/.claude/projects` - the basename must lead with the drive letter. claims.behavior: Claude Code 2.1.258 synthesizes the AskUserQuestion tool_result in `mapToolResultToToolResultBlockParam` from the result object `{questions, answers, response?, annotations?, afkTimeoutMs?}` (the tool's `call()` copies these from the answered tool input; `response` and `afkTimeoutMs` are written only when set) by a fixed branch order: `afkTimeoutMs` set -> `No response after Ns - the user may be away from keyboard ...`, plus `Before going idle the user had selected: <pairs>.` when any answer pair exists; else `response` non-blank -> `The user responded: <response>`; else any answer pair -> `Your questions have been answered: <pairs>. You can now continue with these answers in mind.` when every question was answered by a listed label with no notes, otherwise `The user answered: <pairs>. Read the answers carefully - they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed - and follow what they actually say.`; else `The user did not answer the questions.` A pair renders `"q"="a"`, or `"q"=(no option selected)` when `answers[q]` is the sentinel `(notes only)`, with ` notes: ...` and `selected preview: ...` suffixes from `annotations[q]`. The TUI dialog's submit function returns `updatedInput = {...input, answers, annotations, afkTimeoutMs?}` and never writes `response`: the `Other` entry stores the typed text as `answers[q]`, a notes-only submission stores the `(notes only)` sentinel, `Chat about this` is not an answer at all (it denies the tool use with the `The user wants to clarify these questions.` template, recorded as an `is_error` tool_result), and the idle path is armed by the `askUserQuestionTimeout` setting / `CLAUDE_AFK_TIMEOUT_MS` (default never).
claims.depends: csift recognises an AskUserQuestion answer by EITHER structured signal - a non-empty `toolUseResult.answers` (`has_auq_answers`) OR a present, non-blank `toolUseResult.response` (`has_auq_response`, v0.10.3) - and by the start-anchored text markers as the fallback for carriers without `toolUseResult`; so every shape the TUI produces (a label, an `Other` text, a notes-only sentinel, a partial selection at idle timeout) AND the `response`-only shape (`answers` = {} and the text `The user responded: ...`) classify `user.answer` and open a turn, the `response` shape rendering the questions asked plus a `response:` line in the AUQ unit, and the `Chat about this` deny classifies `user.rejection`. The idle-timeout text with no answer pair (`No response after ...`, `afkTimeoutMs` set) matches no marker and opens no turn. 0.10.0-0.10.2 required a non-empty `answers` and lacked the `The user responded:` prefix, so the `response`-only carrier classified `agent.tool.result` and opened no turn.

pub(crate) fn has_auq_response(&self) -> bool {
        self.tur_probe()
            .as_ref()
            .and_then(|p| p.response.as_ref())
            .and_then(serde_json::Value::as_str)
            .is_some_and(|s| !s.trim().is_empty())
    }
